subjects.Zoology: From the malaria parasite completing its cycle inside a mosquito to the vaccines a laboratory whips up against typhoid, animal biology shows up in Nepal's CEE papers more than most students expect. Zoology carries 40 marks out of 200, and the units stretching between Evolutionary Biology and Human Biology and Physiology are where a focused revision pays off fastest. Two or three of these units - Human Biology and Physiology with its eight organ systems, Microbial Diseases and Immunology with its diseases and vaccines, Animal Diversity and Classification running from Protozoa to Chordata - typically decide the difference between ranks. The pattern is consistent: examiners repeat the same high-yield organs, the same parasite life cycles, the same immune mechanisms year after year. Energy is better spent drilling those repeated themes than skimming every page of the textbook. Start with the unit where your marks are weakest, do a timed set, and check what you misremembered, because that loop is what moves the score line. Pick a unit below and run the questions; the mistakes you make here are the ones you will not make inside the exam hall.
subjects.Botany: Most CEE aspirants treat Botany as the subject to finish off by memorizing names - medicinal plants, tissue types, economic uses - and then face a paper full of process questions instead. That mismatch is the single biggest reason Botany marks slide on exam day. Botany still contributes 40 of the 200 marks, nearly a fifth of what you need to clear the cutoff, and its questions lean on units like Biodiversity, Cell Biology, and Plant Physiology. You will be asked why a C4 plant photosynthesizes differently, how a monocot root differs on a cross-section slide, which fern shows alternation of generations, or which technique regenerates a whole plant from a single cell. None of those can be answered from a memorized one-liner; all of them can be answered if the underlying idea is clear. Keep the names, but anchor every one of them to a function, a diagram, or a comparison. Work unit by unit, do the MCQ sets below, and let the mistakes tell you which idea needs another pass.
subjects.Chemistry: Why does sodium explode the moment it touches water, while the same element bound to chlorine makes a stable table salt? That single curiosity sits at the heart of chemical bonding, the idea that decides half of Chemistry's trickiest MCQs. Chemistry carries 50 marks out of 200 in the CEE paper, and no other subject covers as much ground in one sitting: Physical Chemistry with its stoichiometry, equilibrium and electrochemistry; Organic Chemistry stretching from hydrocarbons to amines; and Inorganic Chemistry's metals, non-metals and their reactions. The quickest way to raise your score is to treat each unit like a checklist - lock the definitions, do the numeric drills, then test yourself under timed conditions. CEE repeats the same nuclei of questions: molarity from titration, half-lives, oxidation states, functional-group reactions. Handle those and the rest becomes pattern recognition. The questions below are built exactly that way, so run them like a real paper, mark your slips, and tighten your weak units before the exam.
subjects.Physics: The algebra you have been solving since lower secondary is the engine room of Physics, yet most CEE aspirants never make that connection consciously. Every Mechanics problem - a projectile's range, a spring's compression, a charged particle's path - is arithmetic dressed up as a story, and the trick is recognizing which formula the story is asking for. Physics pays out 50 marks out of the 200 in the CEE paper, spread across Mechanics, Heat and Thermodynamics, Waves and Optics, and the electricity-heavy units. High scorers are rarely the ones who memorize more; they are the ones who, faced with an unknown quantity, can say what the setup means physically before touching the calculator. Train that habit here. Work through each unit's questions, treat every wrong answer as information about a formula you have not truly placed, then re-test the same unit a day later. The unit list below is arranged to match the exam's own weighting, so start wherever your uncertainty is loudest and move forward question by question.
subjects.MAT: Did you know the 20 marks of the MAT section settle more CEE cutoffs than any science unit of equal weight? Because merit lists are so tight at the top, the Mental Agility Test - Numerical Reasoning, Verbal Reasoning, Logical Sequencing, and spatial puzzles - is where ranks quietly separate. It asks no definitions and no formulas you must memorize; it rewards the mental habits of translating a word problem into arithmetic, spotting the pattern in a series, and reasoning about relations like blood lines or directions. That makes it the fastest section to raise if you practice deliberately: five to ten minutes of MAT-style MCQs daily, with a timer, compounds quickly because the same puzzle engines reappear. Solve the questions below under exam conditions, then scan the solutions to see where your shortcuts went off. Every set you finish here builds the reflex speed that a fixed one-minute-per-question budget demands on the actual paper.

chapters.1: Watch a Nepali satellite engineer release a payload from a spinning upper stage and you are watching Mechanics in action: the release point, the kick, and the drift are all vectors and forces. This unit carries 10 of the 50 Physics marks, and it opens the whole paper, so a shaky start here can pull down your confidence for the hours that follow. The chapter moves from Physical quantities, vectors and scalars through Kinematics and Dynamics into Rotational dynamics, then branches into Fluid statics and dynamics, Circular and Periodic motion, Gravity and Elasticity. Most students find the numeric core of Kinematics and Dynamics the friendliest, while Rotational dynamics and the buoyancy problems in Fluid statics and dynamics are where marks slip. The high-yield habit is to write every given quantity with its unit before you pick a formula, because CEE loves to disguise a missing conversion inside an otherwise easy stem. Mechanics rewards the student who has done five clean problems over the one who has skimmed fifty. Each wrong answer here tells you which equation you misremember or which sign you dropped. Work the questions in order, keep a running list of the equations you had to look up, and close each session with that list in front of you before the quiz below, so the same mistake does not travel to the next unit.
chapters.2: A CEE aspirant will confidently say heat and temperature are the same thing - and then lose a straightforward marks-weighted question that hinges on exactly that difference. Heat is energy in transit; temperature is a reading; the exam tests that distinction early and often. This unit carries 7 of the 50 Physics marks and builds through Thermal energy, heat, temperature and thermometers into Thermal expansion and Quantity of heat, then climbs to the Ideal gas laws and finally the First and Second laws of thermodynamics. The equations are shockingly few - most stems reduce to one or two - but they pair with sign conventions that are easy to fumble. The strongest students treat sign convention as a ritual: they decide the sign before they substitute. They also keep the difference between an isothermal and an adiabatic process separate in their head, because CEE likes to test that boundary with a single word. Practise converting Celsius to Kelvin first, keep the expansion coefficients near your work, and let the quiz below tell you which law you still confuse the direction of. Nobody clears perfect scores here in one sitting; the point is to close the specific gaps this unit exposes before the paper decides your fate.
chapters.3: Why does a guitar string of the same thickness and tension sing a different note than a plucked drumhead? Because one holds a stationary wave and the other a damped one - and that difference is exactly what this unit examines. Waves and Optics carries 8 of the 50 Physics marks and is the most visual chapter on the paper. You will move from Wave motion and Stationary waves into Acoustic phenomena, then shift to light with Reflection, refraction and dispersion, and finish with Interference and Diffraction and polarization. The concept questions reward seeing the pattern in the diagram; the calculation questions reward remembering which slip happens at the interface, since refraction is the single most repeated calculation theme in CEE. Students find Diffraction and polarization the hardest because the qualitative ideas refuse to reduce to a formula, so they survive on mental pictures rather than equations. Treat this chapter as a diagram chapter: trace every ray, label every node and antinode, and name the condition every time you meet it. Let the questions below hammer the distinction between constructive and destructive paths until it is reflexive, because that one reflex earns marks across both the wave questions and the optics questions.
chapters.4: The current that lights your room is the same Physics that charged the capacitor you studied in electrostatics - flow and storage are two sides of one story, and this chapter ties them together. Current Electricity and Magnetism carries 9 of the 50 Physics marks, among the highest in the paper. The route runs from Electrical quantities and Electrical circuits into the Thermoelectric effect, then across Alternating currents to Magnetism, ending with Magnetic properties of materials, Magnetic field and Electromagnetic induction. Circuits dominate: most marks live inside Kirchhoff's rules and the occasional AC waveform question, so fluency with series-parallel reduction decides the score. Students slip most on sign convention when applying induction and on confusing magnetic properties of materials terms like dia-, para- and ferromagnetism. The examiners also love a single-question comparison between heating effect and magnetic effect, which rewards students who read the stem slowly. If you can, sketch the current direction and the field direction on every stem before reading the options - that habit converts half-guesses into confident marks and is exactly the kind of working that shows up again in the applied section of the paper. Once the circuit rules are fluent, the unit stops being a block wall and becomes one of the most dependable sections of the Physics paper you will sit.
chapters.5: Your phone battery marking itself 4.2 V and a lightning flash a few kilometres away are the same idea at wildly different scales: electric charge storing energy in a field. That is this chapter in two lines. Electrostatics and Capacitors carries a modest 4 of the 50 Physics marks, but the questions are unusually predictable, which makes them the cheapest marks on the paper when you prepare them properly. The material stays tight: Capacitors, then Electric charge and electric field, and finally Electric field strength, potential and potential energy. The classic stem gives you charge, plate distance or dielectric, and asks for field strength or potential energy - a three-line calculation that students routinely lose by forgetting the unit conversion or glossing over the dielectric factor. Because the unit is small and its themes repeat, aim for perfection here rather than merely passing. The predictability of the set also means you can safely schedule it late in your revision run, when the formulas are fresh and the pattern is already familiar from the earlier chapters. Run the set below until the capacitor energy and field-strength formulas come out without hesitation, and bank the certainty you will need for the heavier chapters around it.
chapters.6: Examiners love Modern Physics because it is the chapter where the answer cannot be memorized from a guess - the photoelectric effect, the nuclear decay path, and the semiconductor band gap each force a genuine decision about why the experiment behaves the way it does. That is a gift in a rigid exam. Modern Physics carries the largest Physics weightage at 12 of the 50 marks, so it is the difference between a good Physics score and a great one. The chapter crosses Nuclear physics and Radioactivity, spends serious time on the Electron, Photon and photoelectric effect, and then moves through Wave particle duality and X-rays, Solid and semiconductor devices, and closes with Particle physics and recent trends. Fresh aspirants understudy nuclear physics and neglect the photoelectric effect, which is precisely backwards for CEE - the photoelectric effect and semiconductor basics recur with clinical regularity. The strongest students can state the five photoelectric facts the exam builds on: threshold frequency, threshold wavelength, work function, kinetic energy, and the fact that intensity changes count of electrons, not their speed. Solve the questions below with each equation named as you use it; that naming habit is what separates a recalled formula from an applied one on exam day.
chapters.7: Mix vinegar into baking soda and you raise a foam you can exchange for a stoichiometric problem: two reactants, one limiting reagent, and a ratio that decides the gas volume you collect. That is Physical Chemistry summarized in a cup. It is the heaviest unit in the Chemistry paper at 17 of the 50 marks, spanning Basic Concepts in Chemistry and Stoichiometry through Atomic Structure, Classification of Elements and Periodicity, Chemical Bonding and Shape of Molecules, Redox Reaction, States of Matter, Chemical Equilibrium, Volumetric Analysis, Ionic Equilibrium, Chemical Kinetics, Electrochemistry, Chemical Thermodynamics and Nuclear Chemistry. That breadth means depth: most marks cluster in Stoichiometry, equilibrium and electrochemistry, with Volumetric Analysis donating a reliable calculation every year. Students lose marks by skipping units in the middle of that list - Ionic Equilibrium and Redox are often underprepared. The winning habit is to fix each numeric theme once and then rehearse it: molarity, pH, cell potential, equilibrium constant - each is a small ritual that pays repeatedly. Two passes beat ten skims here: first build speed on the standard stems, then attack the twisted ones that CEE uses to separate the top ranks. Once those rituals are locked, the sheer breadth of the unit works in your favour, because the same few equations surface again and again in differently worded stems.
chapters.8: Many CEE students write down every reaction of metals and non-metals as isolated facts, and then cannot answer why sodium displaces hydrogen while gold never will. That 'why' is the periodic trend, and Inorganic Chemistry is the chapter where noticing trends beats memorizing facts. It carries 10 of the 50 Chemistry marks, and its surface area is small - Chemistry of Non-metals, Chemistry of Metals, Bio-inorganic Chemistry - but the stems hide the width of the syllabus behind them. The metals section rewards order: alkali metals first, alkaline earth metals, then the transition elements, each with its characteristic reactions. The high-yield reflex is to read every option through the periodic table: electronegativity explains the halogens, ionization energy explains the s-block, and lattice energy explains almost everything that surprises students here. Bio-inorganic Chemistry is the unit people skip and then regret, because hemoglobin, chlorophyll and vitamin B12 chemistry recur as quiet but dependable marks. Test yourself the way CEE will - on properties, not on exercises. Run the questions below until you can attach a periodic reason to each reaction rather than a memorized sentence, and the facts will finally stay where other students forget them. The reward for that shift in approach is a whole section that most competitors treat as guesswork, simply because they never learned to read through the table.
chapters.9: Why can the same carbon skeleton poison you in one arrangement and sweeten your tea in another? Organic Chemistry is the chapter that answers with structure, and every CEE organic question is really a question about arrangement before it is a question about reaction. It shares the biggest Chemistry weightage with Physical Chemistry at 17 of the 50 marks, so mastery here is non-negotiable for a competitive rank. The route runs from General Organic Chemistry and Hydrocarbons into Aromatic Hydrocarbons, then through Haloalkanes and Haloarenes, Alcohols and Phenols, Ethers, Aldehydes and Ketones, Carboxylic Acid and its Derivatives, Nitro-compounds, Amines and Organometallic Compounds. The high-yield trick is to compare within each family - alcohol versus phenol, aldehyde versus ketone, primary versus tertiary - because the exam rewards differences, not lists. Students lose the most marks on reaction conditions and on misidentifying which carbon the reagent attacks. Draw the skeleton for every stem even when the option looks obvious, and let the quiz below train the reflex. Organic is a chapter you win by naming the mechanism as you go, never by silent memorizing. The functional-group table you build here does double duty across the applied and analytical units, so the effort returns more than a single chapter's worth of marks.
chapters.10: The Haber process you met while studying equilibrium is quietly running the entire fertilizer industry, and the same chemistry is serving the farms of Nepal and India year after year. Applied Chemistry is where the laboratory meets the factory, and CEE uses it to check whether you can connect both. It carries a small weightage of 3 of the 50 Chemistry marks, but those marks are among the most reliably won when you know where to look. The unit covers Manufacturing Processes, Applications of Non-metals, Metals and Compounds, and Chemistry in Service to Mankind - a short list with a friendly character. Students who do well here keep a running list of everyday substances mapped to their chemical identity: baking soda, bleach, lime, plaster of Paris, ammonia. That habit alone answers a surprising fraction of the stems. The unit also rewards a light touch, because the questions rarely dig deep; one clean pass with the set below, matching each product to its process and each chemical name to its common name, is enough to bank the full weightage. Keep the list beside you on the first attempt and read it over once more before the exam - that is genuinely all this unit demands.
chapters.11: A single drop of unknown solution, three test-tubes and a flame - and a trained eye can name the metal at a glance. That is the quiet thrill of Analytical Chemistry, the unit that tests how things are identified rather than made. It carries 3 of the 50 Chemistry marks, small in number but simple to secure. The scope is compact: Chemical Tests, Separation Techniques, and Types of Titration. The classic stems ask whether a salt gives a brick-red flame, which reagent turns iodine blue-black, or which column settles two liquids apart. Students overthink these; the exam pattern is almost ritually stable, so repetition is the whole secret. Learn to recognize the phrase that waves off a test - 'no characteristic colour' - as a clue in itself. Pair that with a clean recall of titration types: acid-base, redox, precipitation, and the indicator each one uses. Run the set below once with the techniques fresh in mind, then again after a gap of a day; the second pass usually turns into an effortless full-score sprint. The same colour and precipitate knowledge quietly reinforces the inorganic unit, so the two chapters train together at no extra cost, and the indicator choices you memorize here are the same ones the volumetric questions of Physical Chemistry lean on.
chapters.12: Examiners love Evolutionary Biology because it packs the grandest story in biology into a chapter where almost every question is a crisp who-study, what-order, when-event item. It carries 3 of the 40 Zoology marks, but the marks are cheap because the syllabus is short and well-defined. The chapter runs from Origin of life and Evidences of evolution through the Theories of evolution and closes with Human evolution. The organic molecules from Miller's flask, the fossil evidence of continental drift, Lamarck versus Darwin on the giraffe's neck, and the hominid sequence - these four clusters repeat across nearly every CEE sitting. The mistake to avoid is reading the theories as dry compare-and-contrast lists; the exam asks which theory is supported by which evidence, and students who connect evidence to theory mark far better. Use the set below to pin each piece of evidence to the theory it supports and each hominid to its defining trait, and the whole chapter closes out in one focused sitting with all its marks banked. A single revision sheet of four lines - origin, evidence, theories, humans - is enough to carry this unit safely into the exam, and it is the rare chapter where the questions feel closer to a story quiz than to biology for once.
chapters.13: Next time you watch a jellyfish pulse in an aquarium, you are looking at an animal that branched away from your own family tree before the backbone even existed. Animal Diversity and Classification is that whole tree in one chapter: the crawl from Protozoa to Chordata that decides 4 of the 40 Zoology marks. The single subtopic, Animal diversity from Protozoa to Chordata, is broad but orderly, and the exam traces it phylum by phylum. Symmetry, body layers, coelom, and segmentation are the four features CEE keeps returning to, so the reliable habit is to read each stem through those four lenses. Students lose marks by memorizing one defining trait per phylum instead of the features that separate similar phyla, such as Platyhelminthes from Nematoda or Annelida from Arthropoda. Draw the phylum ladder once - protozoa, porifera, cnidaria, platyhelminthes, nematoda, annelida, arthropoda, mollusca, echinodermata, chordata - and check each option against the rung. The set below turns that ladder into reflex by drilling the distinguishing features in exactly the order the exam uses. Fill in one example animal per rung from your own knowledge and you have both the ladder and its memory hook in a single page, ready to be recalled within seconds on exam day.
chapters.14: A CEE aspirant, told that a slide shows a striated cell layer, will often write 'skeletal muscle' and collect the mark - then stare at a microscope question about smooth muscle and guess again. Animal Tissues and Histology, the 4-marks unit in Zoology, lives on exactly those micro-differences. The whole chapter is one theme: Types of animal tissues, covering epithelial, connective, muscular and nervous tissue. The exam rewards the four-way comparison: where each tissue sits, what it lines, how its cells are arranged, and which example is classic for it. The classic confusion is striated, unstriated and cardiac muscle, so master that trio first - voluntary versus involuntary, location, and nucleus arrangement. Then fix the epithelia by their lining role, and connective tissue by its matrix. Its compact nature is the real advantage: because the unit is small, perfection is a realistic target. Run the set below and let each missed question expose one distinction; by the time you have done a couple of passes, the tissue map is drawn in your head and the weightage is secure. The same distinctions reappear when you meet the organ systems, so learning this small chapter once saves repeated looks later, and the diagrams themselves become the memory.
chapters.15: What really happens to the earthworm's blood when it breathes through its skin, and why does the frog need three chambers when the lizard has four? Study of Selected Animals answers those by walking one parasite and two animals in detail, and CEE asks about them with devotion. The unit carries 6 of the 40 Zoology marks across three set pieces: Plasmodium, Earthworm (Pheretima), and Frog (Rana). Predictability is the gift here - each prepared animal appears again and again with near-identical figures and facts. For the earthworm, fix the segments, the setae, the nephridia, the typhlosole and the circulatory loop; for the frog, the skin, the heart, the kidneys and the ten pairs of cranial nerves; for Plasmodium, the mosquito host, the liver stage, and the red blood cell cycle. Students who write one clean profile per animal - system by system - always beat those who read the chapter in a single sweep. The set below drills the profiles in exam order, so the answers stop being recollections and become recalls. Because only three organisms are in play, a perfect score is a genuine possibility for anyone who does this unit twice, and each repeated pass shortens the recall time noticeably.
chapters.17: Did you know the body in front of you is already fighting hundreds of microbial invasions that you will never notice? That constant defence is the story of this unit, and CEE asks about it with quiet consistency. Microbial Diseases and Immunology carries 4 of the 40 Zoology marks, and it stays close to three fixed pillars: Microbial diseases, Immunity, and Vaccines. The disease list is the friendliest part - each pathogen pairs with a vector, a symptom, and a control measure, and the exam cycles through the same twenty or so in rotation. Immunity leans on the distinction between innate and acquired defence, and between humoral and cell-mediated paths, which students mislabel more often than they expect. Vaccines reward knowing which one is live, which is killed, and which mobilizes which arm of immunity - this is where the chapter's separate threads finally meet. The reliable method is to learn each disease as a complete card: agent, route, symptom, treatment, and the vaccine if one exists. Run the set below and watch the cards fill quickly, because the chapter's logic is compact and its questions are loyal to the same handful of facts. In one focused sitting this unit can move from a vague worry to a guaranteed four marks, which is a rare return per minute in any paper.
chapters.18: Examiners like Medical Technology and Applied Biology because it connects the classroom to the hospital corridor, and the questions test whether you know which machine does what. It is the smallest unit in Zoology at 2 of the 40 marks, but those two are dependable when the range is this short. The chapter runs across two subtopics only - Medical technology and Applied microbiology - which is precisely why the marks are easy to bank. Medical technology asks about the instruments and the tests: which device measures blood pressure, which imaging method detects a fracture, which laboratory technique grows a culture. Applied microbiology keeps you inside the fermenter, the antibiotic, and the industrial yeasts. Fresh aspirants dread this unit because it seems technical, yet the exam never digs deep - knowing the one-line purpose of each instrument and each microbe covers nearly every stem. Do a single clean pass with the set below, matching equipment to task and microbe to product, and the two marks come home without further effort. Because the whole chapter fits on one revision sheet, you can afford to revisit it the evening before the exam and still keep the bank full, which gives this tiny unit an outsized safety net in your overall Zoology score.
chapters.19: A Himalayan river polluted upstream by a tannery can empty a whole fishing village of its livelihood, which is a painfully real example of why ecology is a life-science chapter and not a soft elective. Biota, Environment and Conservation carries 2 of the 40 Zoology marks, but its questions are current, concrete and easy to score if you read the news as biology. The chapter draws on Animal Behavior, Environmental pollution, Adaptations, and Conservation Biology. Pollution stems name a pollutant and ask for its source or its classic effect - lead, mercury, the greenhouse gases, the ozone depleters - so a short list fixes the whole theme. Adaptations pair an organism with its habitat feature, and Animal Behavior pairs a term with its everyday example, like migration or hibernation. Conservation Biology rewards knowing a few named species and the national or international bodies around them. A quick habit of scanning a Nepali science headline once a week covers most of this unit's news-sensitive stems before you even open a book. The unit is one of the shortest on the paper, which makes perfection feasible; let the set below test you on the exact pollutant-organism-behavior trio the exam prefers, and you will recover marks that many stronger students quietly drop.
chapters.20: A CEE aspirant will spend an hour memorizing every enzyme of glycolysis and still stumble on the simplest stem: which molecule does not come from a carbohydrate, lipid or protein? Basic Components of Life is the chapter that makes such gaps obvious early, at a modest 2 of the 40 Botany marks. Its two subtopics - Carbohydrates, lipids and minerals, then Proteins and enzymes - cover the building blocks everything else in the paper depends on. The exam's favourite tests are the recognition ones: glucose is a hexose, sucrose a disaccharide, starch the storage form; fats are glycerol and fatty acids; egg white and muscle share protein. Where aspirants slip is in the mutual scale - which bond links sugars, which links amino acids, which mineral charges hemoglobin, which enzyme class fits which reaction. Fix the four tables once - carbohydrate, lipid, mineral, protein-enzyme - and answer the stems from analogy rather than memory. The set below is the fastest route to those tables, and its questions preview the vocabulary the heavier Botany chapters will demand of you, which makes these two marks the cheapest groundwork on the Botany paper. Get comfortable here and Cell Biology and Genetics will stop feeling like a vocabulary shock when you reach them.
chapters.21: Why does the same clump of damp soil grow moss on one shaded face and grass on the other? Because each plant sits on a different rung of the classification ladder, and this unit walks that ladder from Monera and Virus all the way to Angiosperms. Biodiversity carries the biggest Botany weightage at 9 of the 40 marks, so it is the chapter to secure properly. The path passes Introduction and classification systems, Monera and Virus, Fungi and Lichens, Algae, Bryophytes, Pteridophytes, Gymnosperms, Angiosperms, Economic importance of plant groups, and Medicinal plants of Nepal - a wide arc, but every rung has a firm hook. The exam rewards the one-line differentiator per group: algae lack true organs, mosses lack vascular tissue, ferns carry them, gymnosperms are naked-seeded, angiosperms protect their seeds in fruits. Nepali context is a quiet bonus here - the Medicinal plants of Nepal subtopic returns year after year with local examples. Build the ladder once, hook an example to each rung, and let the set below convert the classification into reflex marks. The chapter rewards method over memorizing because the same ladder, correctly understood, answers the group questions and the Nepali-context questions alike, so a single afternoon of deliberate practice here returns the largest Botany weightage.
chapters.22: The water cycle you drew in class is, on paper, the same nutrient journey this unit tracks for carbon, nitrogen and phosphorus - except now it is returning to the exam as Ecosystem ecology and Biogeochemical cycles and ecological imbalances. Ecology and Vegetation carries 4 of the 40 Botany marks and rewards the student who already connects it to the pollution theme met in Zoology. The comparison between the lush belts around Kathmandu and the dry scrub of the inner Terai is the same logic the exam photographs from, so read every vegetation stem as a small picture. The three subtopics are tight: Ecosystem ecology, the cycles with their imbalances, and Vegetation and adaptation. The exam asks which organism drives which step of the nitrogen cycle, which term describes a lake's nutrient overload, which vegetation belts sit at which altitude. Aspirants lose marks by learning the cycle stages as lists instead of as a story - who fixes nitrogen, who returns it, who breaks down what. Close the unit by tracing each cycle aloud once, then use the set below to test the connections under time. Because it is compact and overlaps with material you have seen before, these marks come cheap when studied deliberately, leaving more room in your plan for the heavier chapters such as Biodiversity and Cell Biology.
chapters.23: A single litre of living tissue can hold more protein factories than humans have built in a century - few places on the CEE syllabus pack so much per mark as Cell Biology. It carries 5 of the 40 Botany marks, and it is the architect's chapter: everything else in Biotechnology, Genetics and Physiology is built on the same organelles and divisions. The unit moves through Prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells, Cell organelles, and Cell cycle and cell division. The reliable habit is to learn each organelle as a one-line job description with a one-line memory trick: mitochondria are powerhouses, ribosomes make protein, lysosomes digest, and the nucleus keeps the master copy. The division half is where students usually collapse - mitosis versus meiosis, when each occurs, and what each preserves - so name the stage by the event rather than the number. Once the organelle table and the division map are stable, Cell Biology stops being detail and becomes the grammar of the paper. Let the set below stamp those two structures in before moving on, and the later chapters will suddenly read as familiar variations on the same vocabulary, with organelles and stages that keep reappearing in consistent roles throughout the Botany paper.
chapters.24: Examiners keep asking Genetics because one clean Punnett square separates students who rehearse from students who reason, and it is one of the few Botany areas where a calculation style is expected. Genetics carries 6 of the 40 Botany marks, and it behaves like a Numeric Reasoning chapter disguised in biology. The syllabus crosses Genetic material - DNA and RNA, Mendelian Genetics and Linkage, Sex-linked Inheritance, Mutation, and Polyploidy and Genetic Disorders. The DNA half rewards the pairing rules and the three nucleic acid differences; the Mendelian half rewards the ratios - 3:1, 1:1, 9:3:3:1 - and knowing when linkage breaks them apart. Sex-linked Inheritance is the predictable trap: the sons' pattern of transmission sketches the answer. Students lose marks by trying to cram the ratios; the winning method is to rebuild each square on paper, slowly, until the arithmetic becomes second nature. Run the set below square by square, and you will see the same four or five stem shapes return, each one answerable in under a minute. Once the square is a reflex rather than a recital, Genetics turns into one of the least risky units in the whole Botany paper, and the DNA half of the chapter stops being a memory burden.
chapters.25: Slice a celery stalk under a kitchen light and you can watch water climbing through its vascular bundles with a lens - that single sight is the whole point of Plant Anatomy. It carries 3 of the 40 Botany marks, but it sharpens the eye for the other botanical chapters because every diagram in them is sectioned tissue. The unit divides into Plant tissues and vascular bundles, and the Anatomy of monocot and dicot root, stem and leaf. The exam's habit is strictly comparative: rows of monocot on one side, dicot on the other, and four questions about their differences. Students lose marks by memorizing the two lists instead of the logic - the number of cotyledons drives the leaf venation, the root and the vascular pattern, so one trait predicts the rest. Draw the monocot and dicot cross-section side by side once, label the epidermis, cortex, endodermis, xylem and phloem on each, and the comparisons answer themselves. Run the set below to check the labels under exam timing; the unit is compact enough that two passes take it to full marks, and the labelled sections stay vivid for every later chapter that returns to plant structure in the same paper.
chapters.26: A CEE aspirant will revise photosynthesis as a list of products and reactants, and then miss the shorter question that asks what limits the rate on a dry, hot afternoon. Plant Physiology, at 6 of the 40 Botany marks, is where process beats inventory. The unit walks Water relations, Photosynthesis, Respiration, and Plant growth and seed germination. Water relations rewards knowing the path and the forces - root pressure, capillary rise, transpiration pull - and the exam often pairs them against each other. Photosynthesis asks which phase needs light and where each product is made, with C4 versus C3 as the favourite differentiator. Respiration mirrors it, and the comparison of the two is a guaranteed stem every sitting. Seed germination closes the chapter with the classic experiments on light, temperature and water. The mistake is learning each process's map and not its limiting factors; CEE frequently tests which single condition switches a step off. Trace Photosynthesis and Respiration as paired charts once, then let the set below force the limiting-factor questions, and these six marks become steady rather than a gamble. Learn the chapter once properly and it quietly reopens the understanding of Chemistry's respiration-oxidation ideas from a plant's side of the ledger.
chapters.27: How does a pollen grain, carried by a bee, know it must grow a tube that tips its two sperm cells into an ovule that sits a centimetre away? Developmental Botany answers that with the deepest narrowest story on the Botany paper. It carries 2 of the 40 marks and its two subtopics - Reproduction and sporogenesis in angiosperms, then Embryo and endosperm - are small enough to master completely. The exam asks the sequence: meiosis produces the spores, the gametophytes house the gametes, double fertilization unites one sperm with the egg and the other with the polar nuclei. Students who sketch the flowering plant life-cycle once - alternating generations in the angiosperm - answer these stems by pattern rather than by memory. The classic slip is confusing the ploidy: which structure is haploid, which is diploid, which is triploid, and rare students carry that trio loosely into the exam. Fix the cycle and the ploidy in one sitting, run the set below, and walk out with two of the safest marks on the Botany paper. The story is short enough that a single retell the night before the exam keeps the whole sequence in place, and that short story is its own reward to remember.
chapters.28: The technique that rescued a vanishing orchid in a Nepali lab is the same plant tissue culture you met as a one-line fact in Biodiversity; this unit turns it into an applied chapter, and CEE rewards that connection. Applied Botany carries 3 of the 40 marks across Plant tissue culture, Genetic engineering, and Biofertilizers and food security. Tissue culture stems ask why a single cell can regrow a whole plant and which hormone drives shoot or root; the answer lies in totipotency and the auxin-cytokinin ratio, which students memorize better than they understand. Genetic engineering asks the tool-level questions - which enzyme cuts, which joins, which carries - and the exam keeps them to the standard four. Biofertilizers and food security closes with nitrogen fixers, Rhizobium, and the crops they feed. The unit is short, applied and friendly to a methodical student: learn each technique as a purpose plus the one tool or hormone that makes it work, run the set below, and bank the three marks without a textbook marathon. It is also the chapter that makes Biotechnology questions in the sciences section feel familiar rather than alien on exam day, and that reassurance is worth its weight in marks.
chapters.29: Most CEE aspirants expect the MAT to be pure puzzles, so they are genuinely surprised that a fifth of it is arithmetic that older competitive exams have been recycling for decades - and that predictability is exactly the opportunity. Numerical Reasoning carries 5 of the 20 MAT marks and is the easiest section to convert into guaranteed points. The syllabus holds ten classics: Time and Work, Percentage, Profit and Loss, Ratio and Proportion, Problem on Ages, Averages, Time, Speed and Distance, Permutation and Combination, Partnership, and Simple Interest and Compound Interest. Each one reduces to one or two standard formulas, and the exam reuses the same stem skeletons, so pattern recognition takes over fast. The winning routine is timed practice: set a stopwatch, solve the formula questions first, and save the wordier ones for the second pass. Students lose marks to panic arithmetic more than to ignorance, so the habit of writing the formula before substituting is what separates scores. Work the set below against the clock, compare the methods in the solutions, and the five marks resolve into statistical certainties. A single week of ten-minute daily drills is enough to notice the difference in your own instinct for which formula a stem is hiding.
chapters.30: Examiners like Verbal Reasoning because it tests the language skill the whole CEE is quietly measuring - the ability to read a relationship and follow it through - and it does so in very few marks. Verbal Reasoning carries 5 of the 20 MAT marks, and its stems are friendlier than their reputation suggests. The unit spans Distance and Direction, Coding and Decoding, Ranking Order, Verbal Classification, Verbal Analogy, Synonym and Antonym, Verbal Puzzle, Blood Relations, Statement and Reasons, and Arithmetical Operation. The trick that unlocks almost everything is to slow the reading: most wrong invites come from rushing past a keyword like 'left' instead of 'right', or 'father' instead of 'uncle'. For coding and analogy stems, the method is to name the relationship aloud before hunting the option. Students who build a habit of drawing blood lines and direction grids on the rough sheet answer these with cold confidence. Run the set below at a deliberate pace, review every skip in the solutions, and let the patterns teach you the rest; the five marks are among the gentlest you can bank here. The same relationship-spotting reflex quietly feeds the Synonym, Antonym and puzzle stems elsewhere in the MAT, so the effort spent here never stays inside a single chapter.
chapters.31: The next time you wait for a kettle to boil and notice the shop sign repeats its digits in a sequence, you are doing what this unit formalizes: spotting the rule, then predicting the next item. Logical Sequencing carries 5 of the 20 MAT marks, and it is the section where speed is won honestly, by recognizing the pattern family rather than grinding each stem. The syllabus runs Number Series, Alphabet Series, Continuous Patterns and Positional Series, Matrix and Missing Characters, Analogy, Classification, Logical Sequence of Words, Logical Venn-Diagram, and Common Properties. Number series rewards scanning the differences first - add, subtract, multiply, alternate - because a surprising share of stems fall into one of four progression shapes. Alphabet series borrow the same eyes with a shift to letter positions, and Venn diagrams turn into set logic you already know from everyday grouping. The discipline that scores is to attempt the pattern stem in the first ten seconds, skip cleanly if the family is unclear, and return later with fresh eyes. Time the set below, review the missed families, and watch the speed curve flatten toward a perfect section. The pattern vocabulary you build here - difference scanning, letter shifts, set overlap - carries straight into the Spatial chapter that follows it in the paper.
chapters.32: A CEE aspirant looking at a cube-and-dice question will often rotate the paper in the air and lose the answer somewhere between the two views; the better habit is to fix one face and walk the adjacent faces in writing. Spatial Relation and Abstract Reasoning carries 5 of the 20 MAT marks and rewards exactly that kind of patient, diagram-drawing method. The unit collects Figure Formation, Construction of Figure, Grouping Figure, Paper Folding, Cube and Dice, Embedded Figure, Dot Situation, Water Image and Mirror Image, and pairs them with Series, Classification Test, Analogy, Matrix and Analytic Reasoning Test. The figure questions all fall into a small family of moves - rotate, reflect, combine, embed - and recognizing which move a stem wants beats any amount of staring. Water and mirror images reduce to a left-right or top-bottom swap, which students mark wrong by forgetting the axis the stem specifies. The winning routine is to sketch every move on paper, one step at a time, and never trust the mental image alone. Run the set below with paper nearby, review each skipped shape in the solutions, and the abstract section turns methodical rather than mysterious. With practice your eye learns to announce the move - rotate, reflect, combine - before your hand even begins the sketch, which is the real skill this chapter is grading.
chapters.16: You already know the blood flows to the heart and the food goes to the stomach; this unit just plants a microscope on every one of those familiar organs. Human Biology and Physiology carries the heaviest Zoology weightage at 15 of the 40 marks, so it is the chapter that separates serious Zoology scores. The syllabus runs through the Digestive System, Respiratory System, Circulatory System, Excretory System, Nervous System, Sense Organs, Endocrinology and the Reproductive System. Each system contributes its own cluster: the pathway of each, the enzymes at each station, the hormones controlling it, and the one or two classic disorders. The exam rewards the pathway style - trace the journey - over isolated facts, so practice by narrating each route aloud once: digestion from mouth to anus, circulation from vena cava to aorta, impulses from receptor to effector. Students lose marks by mixing hormone sources and by forgetting which enzyme acts at which pH. Work the set below system by system and you will convert the heaviest Zoology unit into your most dependable marks. Finish each system in the same session you started it so the pathway and its enzymes arrive together rather than as loose fragments, and the unit quickly becomes the backbone of your whole Zoology revision.

subchapters.1|Physical quantities, vectors and scala: Choose between measuring the length of a room and the wind pushing a kite, and you will reach for a ruler in one case and a compass in the other - that instinct is the whole of this topic. Physical quantities are the measurable properties of nature, and they split into scalars, which carry only size, and vectors, which carry both size and direction. Distance, speed and mass are scalars; displacement, velocity and force are vectors. The exam's favourite questions hinge on which is which and how they combine, because two vectors add differently than two scalars do. This difference feeds directly into Kinematics and Dynamics, where projectile paths and net forces are vector problems dressed in everyday words. The reliable habit is to read the stem for direction words - towards, opposite, at an angle - before you touch a formula, because that single read decides the arithmetic. Try the questions below and watch how often the answer hides in the scalar-versus-vector distinction.
subchapters.1|Kinematics: A CEE aspirant booking a bus from Kathmandu to Pokhara will quote the kilometres without a thought, yet fumbles whether that number is a distance or a displacement on the exam paper. This is the bridge topic: Kinematics, the study of motion without asking what causes it. Its four quantities - distance, displacement, speed, velocity - share three equations that power nearly every stem. The classic trap is the free-fall sign: when a ball is thrown up, students drop the negative sign on the way down and lose the mark. Acceleration in free fall is constant, and the equation set connects displacement with velocity and time in a tight loop. The topic then hands off cleanly to Dynamics, which adds the force that Kinematics deliberately ignores, and to Circular and Periodic motion, which repeats the same equations on a curved path. Lock the three kinematic equations and the sign convention once, and every motion question below becomes a substitution exercise rather than a puzzle.
subchapters.1|Dynamics: What actually makes a sprinter accelerate out of the blocks, and why does a heavier car need a bigger push to match a lighter one? The answer is Newton, and that answer is this topic. Dynamics is the study of force and its effect on motion, built on three laws that CEE asks about in near-identical forms year after year. Inertia, the first law, explains why your body lurches forward when a bus brakes; the second law turns that into the formula force equals mass times acceleration; the third law is the action-reaction pair that students misquote more than any other line in Physics. Friction sits at the heart of the topic, and the stem almost always involves it: a block on a slope, a box pushed across a floor. The topic leans on Kinematics for its equations but changes the question from what happens to why, and it feeds Rotational dynamics by exchanging linear force for torque. Nail the third law's phrasing and the friction coefficient in the set below, and Dynamics stops being the chapter people fear.
subchapters.1|Rotational dynamics: Spin a bicycle wheel in the air on your finger and it stays stubbornly upright while you wobble beneath it - that stubbornness is the same Physics that opens a door, tightens a bolt and balances a dancer. Rotational dynamics is the study of rotation, the mirror of the linear dynamics you already know: mass becomes moment of inertia, force becomes torque, and momentum becomes angular momentum. The exam rewards the pairings, because a stem will ask which formula changes and which stays when a wheel's radius shrinks. Students slip on two things: the moment of inertia's dependence on where the mass sits, and the direction of the torque that produces rotation. The topic differs from Dynamics by keeping the conversation circular, but it reuses the same energy and momentum ideas. If you can state why a ballet dancer pulls her arms in to spin faster - conservation of angular momentum - you can answer half the stems here. Work the questions below with torque direction in mind and the rotation suddenly feels linear again.
subchapters.1|Fluid statics and dynamics: The reason a ship made of steel floats while a dropped steel coin sinks is not weight but displaced water - Archimedes' insight, and the quiet engine of this whole topic. Fluid statics and dynamics covers liquids at rest and in motion, and its two star ideas are pressure and buoyancy. Pressure is force spread over area, which is why a needle pierces skin while a fingertip cannot; buoyancy is the upthrust equal to the weight of displaced fluid. The exam loves the submerged-object questions: whether an object sinks, floats or hangs midway depends on comparing its density with the fluid's. Pascal's principle and the continuity of flow for moving fluids complete the topic's small toolkit. It connects to Dynamics through the forces involved in submerged bodies and to Elasticity through the way most fluids share the idea of stress without shearing. Once density comparison becomes a reflex, the stems below answer themselves, because nearly every one reduces to weight versus upthrust.
subchapters.1|Circular and Periodic motion: A stone whirled on a string, a planet orbiting the Sun, and a pendulum swinging off a clock face all repeat the same idea: motion that comes back around. Circular and Periodic motion is the study of those paths, and the exam treats it as one theme with two halves. Circular motion asks why an object moving in a circle is always accelerating - the constant pull toward the centre - and the centripetal force formula decides the answers. Periodic motion brings the pendulum and the spring, where displacement, time period and frequency form the observable trio. Students commonly mix frequency with time period and forget that period is time, not cycles. The topic leans on the Kinematics equations for speed and on Rotational dynamics for the spokes analogy, and it is the physical root of the waves that follow. Lock each formula's name with its unit and the stems below start reading as pattern recognition, because the exam repeats the same circular scenarios every year.
subchapters.1|Gravity: Jump off a step and you are already in free fall, the same acceleration Galileo measured from a tower and Newton later explained with an inverse-square law. Gravity is the force that threads every science on the paper, and this topic gives it its mechanics. The core statement is Newton's law: force weakens with the square of distance, so an object twice as far feels a quarter of the force. The exam pairs that law with the acceleration due to gravity, which changes with height and depth, and with the orbits that combine gravity with circular motion. Students lose marks thinking gravity acts only on the ground - it acts on satellites, moons and objects on the table alike. The topic connects directly to Circular and Periodic motion through satellites, and to Fluid statics through the weight that determines buoyancy. Nail the inverse-square phrasing and the two equations for g, and the questions below stop being exotic: they are just Mechanics wearing a planetary costume.
subchapters.1|Elasticity: Stretch a rubber band, release it, and watch it snap back - that recoverable behaviour has a name, a formula and a full set of CEE questions. Elasticity is the branch of Mechanics that studies how materials deform under force and return to shape. The two central quantities are stress, the force per area, and strain, the fractional change in length, and the ratio between them is the modulus of elasticity. Hooke's law, the topic's keystone, states that extension is proportional to load within a limit, which is why a spring balance works at all. The exam asks which material stretches most for a given force, and whether a wire's modulus changes when it thickens - the answer, no, surprises many. The topic joins Fluid statics through the idea of stress, and it is the practical side of gravity: a hanging wire's extension mixes Hooke's law with the weight. Fix stress against strain once and the questions below reveal their single repeated shape: load, extension, modulus.
subchapters.2|Thermal energy, heat, temperature and: Hold a metal spoon in a hot cup of tea and the spoon end warms up while the tea stays put - that everyday transfer is the boundary this topic draws between heat and temperature. Heat is thermal energy moving between bodies, and temperature is the reading that tells you which way it flows. The three scales matter too: Celsius, Fahrenheit and Kelvin, with Kelvin as the true measure used in gas problems. The exam's classic stem gives a thermometer or a conversion question, and students lose marks on the unit conversions and on forgetting that a thermometer reads temperature but does not add heat. The topic feeds directly into Thermal expansion, where the same rising temperature changes lengths and volumes, and into Quantity of heat, which puts numbers on the transfer. Fix the three scale formulas and the heat-versus-temperature sentence, and every stem below resolves into a unit check plus a direction call.
subchapters.2|Thermal expansion: Leave a metal lid on a jam jar under hot sun and the reason it turns freely is expansion - the entire lid grew slightly with the temperature before your hand did. Thermal expansion is that change in size under heat, and it shows up in bridges, rails and thermometers alike. Solids expand in length, area and volume; liquids and gases expand in volume too, with gases doing so most dramatically. The formula gives the change as a product of the original length, the coefficient of expansion and the temperature rise, and the exam asks which material expands most or which part of a bimetallic strip bends where. Students mix linear and volume coefficients, forgetting the factor of three. The topic leans on Thermal energy for the idea of what the temperature change means and hands off to Quantity of heat for the energy involved. Stay alert to the coefficient's units in the set below and the answers stop hiding behind the arithmetic.
subchapters.2|Quantity of heat: Boiled a litre of water twice the time of half a litre, and you know instinctively that heat and mass go together - Quantity of heat just puts numbers on that instinct. The topic gives the energy needed to change a body's temperature, through the specific heat capacity, and the energy to change its state, through latent heat. The exam asks the melting and vaporization questions constantly: how much ice melts in warm water, why steam burns worse than boiling water, what cools a drink fastest. The two trap words are latent, which means hidden because no temperature change shows. Students lose marks by using specific heat when the substance is changing state, so reading whether the substance melts, freezes, boils or condenses decides the formula. The topic connects to Thermal energy by giving its heat its numbers, and to Thermal expansion by sharing the same dependence on temperature. Call the state change before you calculate in the set below, and the stems lay themselves out.
subchapters.2|Ideal gas: Pump a bicycle tyre in the sun and it stiffens twice: once from the added air, once from the heat - two of the three ways gas responds that this topic formalizes. The ideal gas replaces real molecules with a simplifying model: point particles in constant random motion, no attraction between them, perfectly elastic collisions. That model produces the one formula that connects pressure, volume and temperature. The exam loves the three fixed-state cases - constant temperature, constant pressure, constant volume - which reduce the gas law to simpler proportionalities. Students confuse which stays constant in each case, so they invert the relation and lose the mark. The topic builds on Thermal energy for the meaning of temperature and links to the First law of thermodynamics, which follows the gas as it expands and does work. Name the fixed quantity first in the set below, then let the proportionality decide, and the gas questions become almost automatic.
subchapters.2|First law of thermodynamics: Stretch a rubber band fast and it feels warm; release it and it cools - energy is moving in and out, and the First law of thermodynamics keeps that accounting straight. The law states that the heat added to a system equals the increase in its internal energy plus the work it does on its surroundings, a single sentence that guards the exam's most repeated sign questions. The sign convention is where students fall: heat added is positive, heat lost is negative, work done by the gas is positive, work done on the gas is negative. Read four signs, substitute, and the answer surfaces. The topic leans on the Ideal gas law for the work term, since work depends on pressure and volume change, and it connects to Quantity of heat through the heat term. The set below is built to drill exactly that sign ritual, and once the convention is automatic, the First law stops being the thermodynamics chapter's fear point.
subchapters.2|Second law of thermodynamics: A dropped cup never reassembles itself, and heat never flows uphill from a cold drink to a warm hand - both are the Second law of thermodynamics, the exam's favourite qualitative idea in physics. While the First law says energy is conserved, the Second law says not every conserved flow is possible: heat moves spontaneously from hot to cold, and no cyclic engine can convert all its heat into work. The exam tests this with phrase-level questions - which statement describes the law, which machine obeys it, which process violates it - and with the concept of entropy, the measure of disorder that never decreases in a closed system. Students try to fit the Second law into a formula and lose the conceptual stems. The topic stays attached to the First law through the engine that takes in heat and does work, but where the First law counts energy, the Second law rules direction. Practise identifying the forbidden process in the set below and this topic becomes free marks.
subchapters.3|Wave motion: Drop a stone in a pond and the ripples travel outward while the water itself barely moves - that is the difference at the heart of all waves, and it is where this topic begins. Wave motion is the transfer of energy without the transfer of matter, and the exam checks it through two families: mechanical waves that need a medium, and electromagnetic waves that do not. The core vocabulary is a tight set - wavelength, frequency, amplitude, speed - joined by the single relation that speed equals frequency times wavelength. Students stumble most on the transverse-versus-longitudinal difference and on which direction each part of the medium moves. The topic feeds Stationary waves, which form where two waves meet, and Acoustic phenomena, which put waves into sound. Match each quantity to its unit in the set below, and the wave question that once felt abstract becomes a straight substitution with a drawing attached.
subchapters.3|Stationary waves: Pluck a guitar string and the whole string trembles in fixed loops, not as one moving bump - those stable loops are stationary waves, and this topic explains why they look frozen. A stationary wave forms when two identical waves travel in opposite directions and interfere, producing regions called nodes that never move and antinodes that always do. The exam asks how many loops fit a string, where the nodes lie, and what happens when frequency changes, with the relation between string length and wavelength deciding it. Students confuse nodes with antinodes and misread the loop count from the diagram. The topic stands on Wave motion for its travelling waves but adds the pattern, and it connects to Acoustic phenomena, where the same standing pattern in a tube or pipe produces musical notes. Count the loops and mark the nodes in every diagram in the set below, and the stationary wave picture becomes permanently clear.
subchapters.3|Acoustic phenomena: Standing near a running bus, you hear its pitch rise as it approaches and fall as it leaves - the Doppler effect, the crowd-pleaser of Acoustic phenomena. This topic turns the wave ideas of the unit into the physics of sound: how pitch relates to frequency, loudness to amplitude, and how the medium carries the wave. The exam's reliable stems are the Doppler questions that ask whether the observed pitch rises or falls, the echo and reflection versions, and the speed-of-sound calculations in air. Students lose marks by deciding the Doppler direction with the wrong sign, and by forgetting that sound needs a medium where light does not. The topic leans on Stationary waves through the musical notes in pipes and strings, and on Wave motion for the general wave behavior. Fix the Doppler rule - toward means higher pitch, away means lower - and most of the set below answers itself on a single read.
subchapters.3|Reflection, refraction and dispersion: A pencil slanting in a glass of water looks bent where the waterline meets it, but the pencil is straight - light changed direction at the surface, and that change is this topic. Reflection, refraction and dispersion cover light's behaviour at boundaries: reflection bounces it back, refraction bends it as it enters a new medium, and dispersion splits white light into colours. The exam's favourite calculation is Snell's law through the refractive index, and its favourite concept question asks why white light spreads into a rainbow. Students slip on which medium bends the ray steeply - the larger index wins - and on the total internal reflection boundary that decides when a ray escapes entirely. The topic connects to Interference and Diffraction, which also rely on waves of light, and it follows Wave motion's theme of energy travelling through a medium. Identify the boundary and the index direction first in the set below, and the optics stems resolve cleanly.
subchapters.3|Interference: The shimmering colours on a soap bubble are not paint but waves of light cancelling and adding in thin layers - that effect has a name in this topic: interference. Interference is what happens when two waves overlap, reinforcing where they meet in step and cancelling where they meet out of step. The exam's classic is the two-slit experiment: bright fringes appear where the path difference is a whole number of wavelengths, and dark fringes where it is a half. The reliable approach is to identify whether the stem wants constructive or destructive interference, then compare the path difference to the wavelength count. Students confuse the two conditions, so the fringe type comes out inverted. The topic builds on Wave motion's overlap idea and pairs directly with Diffraction and polarization for the full wave-nature story. State the path difference in wavelengths before you choose in the set below, and the fringe questions lose their sting.
subchapters.3|Diffraction and polarization: Hold two fingers close together and look at a distant lamp through the gap, and the slit seems narrower than it is - light is bending around the edge, the everyday sign of diffraction. Diffraction is light spreading when it passes an obstacle or aperture, and polarization is the filtering of those waves to one plane of vibration. The exam asks which condition widens the diffraction pattern - a narrower slit - and which direction a polarizer blocks, with sunglasses and 3D glasses as the classic examples. Students find these stems hard because the ideas are qualitative, so they try to force a formula that is rarely there. The topic follows Interference as the third piece of the wave evidence for light, and it connects to Reflection and refraction through the same boundary surfaces. Read every option as a picture rather than a number in the set below, and the qualitative stems stop being a source of doubt.
subchapters.4|Electrical quantities: Flip a switch and the light answers instantly, yet the individual charges crawl through the wire - the difference between flow rate and the flow itself is more than a curiosity; it is this topic. Electrical quantities define the measuring of current, voltage, resistance and charge, along with their units and the relationships between them. Current is the rate of charge flow, potential difference is the energy per charge that pushes it, and resistance is the opposition the wire offers. Ohm's law ties them into the formula that opens every circuit problem. Students lose early marks by mixing charge and current and by forgetting which quantity the ammeter and the voltmeter read. The topic is the foundation for Electrical circuits, where these quantities are applied to combinations, and for the Thermoelectric effect, which creates a small voltage from heat. Name the instrument and the quantity it measures in the set below, and the definitions stop being a guessing game.
subchapters.4|Electrical circuits: Read the label on any household appliance - voltage, wattage, frequency - and you are reading a circuit's spec sheet, which is exactly the language this topic speaks. Electrical circuits take the quantities from the previous topic and put them to work in combinations, asking how current splits between branches and how resistance adds when devices are wired together. The reliable method is circuit reduction: resistors in series add their values, resistors in parallel add their reciprocals, and the whole network collapses to one equivalent resistance. The exam also likes the safety and power questions - why a fuse blows, what wattage a bulb draws. Students slip by applying the series formula to parallel branches and losing the reciprocal step. The topic depends on Ohm's law and the electrical quantities that define each component, and it feeds the Alternating currents theme that follows. Reduce the network step by step in the set below, and the circuit questions become tidy arithmetic.
subchapters.4|Thermoelectric effect: Touch two different metal wires twisted together at one end while a volunteer holds the other end, and a tiny current runs that nobody supplied - heat has become electricity, and that is the thermoelectric effect. When two dissimilar metals join and their junctions sit at different temperatures, a small voltage appears, the principle behind thermocouples that measure furnace heat. The exam keeps to the essentials: which junction temperatures produce the current, which metal pair is common, and how the effect compares with the heating and magnetic effects of a current. Students rarely study this one seriously, which makes it a quiet differentiator when it appears. The topic connects to Electrical quantities through the voltage it generates, and to Electrical circuits as a practical current source. Fix the single condition - two different metals, different temperatures - and the stems below become the simplest free marks in the unit.
subchapters.4|Alternating currents: The socket on your wall delivers current that reverses direction fifty times a second, which is why the lamp glows steadily despite the constant switching - that invisible reversal is alternating current. This topic examines AC, the standard of the power grid, against direct current that flows one way. The key vocabulary is root-mean-square, the effective value that lets AC be compared with DC for the same heating effect, and frequency, the number of reversals per second. The exam asks for the peak-versus-rms relation, and the grid voltage of 220 V is in fact the rms value, a fact that quietly surprises. Students lose marks by treating AC peak as if it were the everyday figure. The topic stands on the circuit ideas of the earlier unit and hands the full wave behaviour to the electromagnetic themes that follow. Note whether a stem quotes peak or rms in the set below, and the alternating current questions turn methodical.
subchapters.4|Magnetic properties of materials: Slap a fridge magnet on the door and it holds all day, but slide a copper coin near it and nothing happens - the materials' magnetic response, and this topic's whole question. Magnetic properties of materials sorts substances by how they react in a field: ferromagnetic materials like iron take up magnetism strongly, paramagnetic materials weakly, and diamagnetic materials subtly oppose the field. The exam asks which category a named material falls in, and which material is used for a transformer core or a permanent magnet. Students confuse the three categories and misremember the classic examples, especially the odd pairs like bismuth and copper. The topic connects to the Magnetic field that precedes it and to Electromagnetic induction through the cores that concentrate it. Book the material list once - iron for ferro, aluminium for para, copper for dia - and the set below turns into a clean matching exercise.
subchapters.4|Magnetic field: Sprinkle iron filings around a bar magnet and they arrange themselves into curving lines between the poles - those lines are the magnetic field, and reading them is this topic. The magnetic field is the region where a magnetic force acts, mapped by field lines that run from north to south. The exam asks about the force on a moving charge and on a current-carrying wire, both governed by direction rules that students dread, and about which field shape surrounds which arrangement of magnets. The three-finger rules for force direction are the highest-yield skill because nearly every current-and-field stem hinges on them. The topic builds on Electrical circuits through the current that creates and feels magnetic effects, and it precedes Magnetic properties of materials, which sorts by field response. Practise the force-direction rules with your own hand in the set below, and the magnetic stems lose their fear entirely.
subchapters.4|Electromagnetic induction: Pedal a dynamo-powered bicycle lamp and the faster you go, the brighter the light - motion across a magnetic field has become a current, the phenomenon of electromagnetic induction. When a conductor moves through a magnetic field, or the field through the conductor changes, a voltage is induced that drives a current, the principle behind every generator on the grid. The exam asks the two ways induction happens, the direction of the induced current, and Lenz's law, which states the induced effect opposes its own cause. Students lose marks on the direction and on forgetting that a steady field induces nothing by itself - change is required. The topic stands on the Magnetic field for its source and on Alternating currents for what generators produce. Look for the word changing in every stem in the set below; where there is no change, there is no induction, and that sentence answers half the questions.
subchapters.5|Electric charge and electric field: Rub a plastic comb through your hair in winter and it lifts paper bits - you have separated charge, and the leftover force field is this topic's opening act. Electric charge is the property that makes objects attract or repel, and the electric field is the region of influence around a charge that exerts force on others. The exam pairs the two: like charges repel, unlike attract, and the field radiates outward from positive charges and inward toward negative ones. The reliable calculation is the force between two charges, which dilutes with the square of the distance exactly like gravity, and the drawing question asks which way a field arrow points. Students lose marks by forgetting that field direction means the push on a positive test charge. The topic builds into Electric field strength and potential and links to Capacitors, which store that field's energy. Mark the sign of every charge in the set below and the attractions and repulsions resolve instantly.
subchapters.5|Electric field strength, potential and: Stand under a high-voltage tower and the air around you charges with a field you cannot feel - but the math of that invisible field is precisely this topic. Electric field strength measures how hard the field pushes a charge, potential measures the energy per charge, and potential energy the stored energy of the arrangement. The exam asks which quantity changes when distance doubles, and the field-versus-potential difference: field is force per charge, potential is energy per charge, and students swap the two definitions at their cost. The classic stem places a charge between two plates and asks for the force or the energy; the geometry of parallel plates keeps the field uniform and the arithmetic simple. The topic builds directly on Electric charge and electric field and precedes Capacitors, which bank the energy. Label force and energy on every option in the set below, and the two definitions stop colliding inside your head.
subchapters.5|Capacitors: Your phone battery holds charge, but a separate component in the same phone - the capacitor - stores energy in an electric field far faster, which is why it smooths every sudden flash and pulse. Capacitors are two conductors separated by an insulator, storing energy as a field between their plates. The exam's core question is the capacitance formula, which grows with plate area and shrinks with separation, and how a dielectric - the insulator between the plates - multiplies the storage. The most-repeated stem gives charge, voltage or plate geometry and asks for the stored energy, often with a unit trap. Students confuse the factor of a half in the energy formula and forget that a dielectric changes everything. The topic follows Electric field strength and potential, whose voltage drives the storage, and it closes the electricity sequence that ends this unit. Note whether the stem asks charge, voltage or energy in the set below, and the capacitor questions become tidy arithmetic.
subchapters.6|Nuclear physics: Every atom in your body carries a nucleus a hundred thousand times smaller than the atom itself, yet that speck carries nearly all the mass - and this topic is the study of that crowded centre. Nuclear physics deals with the structure of the nucleus and the forces that hold it together, introducing the proton, the neutron and the binding energy that explains why lone protons repel but a packed nucleus holds. The exam asks which force binds the nucleus at close range, how mass number and atomic number change in a decay, and the notation that labels each nucleus. Students lose marks on the neutron count and for confusing mass number with atomic number. The topic hands directly to Radioactivity, which applies the nucleus rules in decay chains, and connects to Electron and photon themes through the energy released. Practise reading a nuclear notation line by line - top mass, bottom charge - and the stems below become a code you already know.
subchapters.6|Electron: The cathode-ray television that once filled living rooms was, in essence, a laboratory demonstration of the electron, and this topic is where the particle gets properly introduced. Electron deals with the discovery, charge and mass of the electron, along with the experiments that measured them, and the behaviour of the particle as it moves through electric and magnetic fields. The exam asks which experiment measured the charge, what ratio a famous tube demonstrated, and how a beam deflects between charged plates. Students remember the quantities but mix up which experiment produced which number. The topic feeds the Photon and photoelectric effect, where electrons absorb light energy and leave the surface, and it connects to the Wave particle duality that follows as the electron's double identity. Fix the two classic results - the charge and the mass - in the set below, and the electron questions stop feeling like history and start feeling like arithmetic.
subchapters.6|Photon and photoelectric effect: Point a violet light at a zinc plate and electrons leap off it, but shine a brighter red light and none move at all - intensity cannot override colour, and that surprising fact cleared the way for this topic. The photoelectric effect shows that light ejects electrons only when its frequency passes a threshold, so the light acts like packets of energy called photons. The exam loves this pairing: the energy of a photon rises with frequency, and the emitted electron's kinetic energy depends on the photon energy minus the binding work function. Students lose marks on the two simplest facts - brighter light releases more electrons but not faster ones, and red light of any brightness cannot start the effect below the threshold. The topic feeds Wave particle duality, where light's particle nature is settled, and connects to the Electron through the atoms it frees. Fix the threshold language first in the set below, and the photoelectric stem almost predicts its own answer.
subchapters.6|Wave particle duality and X-rays: Light that bends through a slit like a water wave also knocks electrons out of a metal like a hail of bullets - it is both, and this topic is where Physics agreed to accept that contradiction. Wave particle duality accepts that light and matter show wave behaviour and particle behaviour depending on the experiment.
