The topic rests on Genetic material and Cell division, whose chromosomes carry the alleles, and it hands Sex-linked Inheritance the same logic. Draw the square and count the boxes in the set below, and the Mendelian stems resolve into the ratios they were born as.
subchapters.24|Sex-linked Inheritance: A trait passed from a colour-blind grandfather to a grandson through a perfectly normal daughter reveals that some genes ride the sex chromosomes - the mechanism this topic isolates. Sex-linked Inheritance studies the genes on the X and Y chromosomes, why a recessive allele shows in males with a single X, and how conditions like color blindness and hemophilia follow their distinctive family patterns. The exam asks which parent passes a defective X, why males express the trait more often, and what ratio a named cross produces. Students lose marks by treating the sex chromosomes as identical to autosomes or by ignoring the father's single X. The topic is a special case of Mendelian Genetics, modified by the X and Y, and it connects back to the Cell division chapter's gametes. Track which X travels where in each cross in the set below, and the sex-linked stems resolve through the parents' chromosomes alone.
subchapters.24|Mutation, Polyploidy and Genetic Diso: A single letter changed in a word can turn a whole sentence into nonsense, and the same is true of a gene: one changed base can produce a disorder - the consequences this topic gathers. Mutation, Polyploidy and Genetic Disorders covers the changes in DNA that create new alleles, the polyploid conditions where entire chromosome sets multiply, and the human genetic disorders from sickle-cell anemia to Down syndrome. The exam asks which disorder matches which genetic cause, whether a mutation is a base change or a chromosome change, and what chromosome count a named condition carries. Students lose marks by tying a disorder to the wrong chromosome or gene. The topic builds on the Mendel and linkage work, applying its logic to errors, and it connects to Genetic material through the DNA changes at the root. Link each disorder to its cause once in the set below - one base, one chromosome - and the disorder stems file into two clean drawers.
subchapters.25|Plant tissues and vascular bundles: A tree's height, a leaf's rigidity and a stem's transport all depend on its internal plumbing, and the cells that build that plumbing are the plant tissues this topic lays out. Plant tissues and vascular bundles sorts the tissues of plants: the meristem that keeps growing, the simple tissues like parenchyma, collenchyma and sclerenchyma, and the vascular bundles that bundle xylem and phloem for water and food transport. The exam asks which tissue does which job, how the vascular bundle is arranged in a stem, and which tissue is living or dead at maturity. Students lose marks by confusing xylem with phloem or the bundle's arrangement between stem and root. The topic opens Plant Anatomy and feeds the next entry's root-stem-leaf survey, where the tissue plan becomes visible. Match each tissue to its duty in the set below - transport, support, growth - and the anatomy stems arrange into an ordered cross-section.
subchapters.25|Anatomy of monocot and dicot root, st: Cut a stem across and the rings you see are the footprints of a year, but cut a monocot and dicot stem side by side and the difference is visible in a single glance - scattered bundles versus an ordered ring. Anatomy of monocot and dicot root, stem and leaf compares the internal arrangements of the two great flowering-plant families, from the root's central cylinder to the leaf's layered mesophyll. The exam asks which arrangement marks a monocot or a dicot, how the vascular bundle differs in each, and which tissue layer a named structure sits in. Students lose marks by relabeling the stem's bundle order or the root's vascular pattern. The topic applies Plant tissues and vascular bundles to real organs, completing the Plant Anatomy chapter. Sketch the three cross-sections once in the set below - ring, scattered, central - and the monocot-dicot questions answer from the pattern alone.
subchapters.26|Water relations: A tall tree pulls water to its topmost leaf against gravity without a single pump, and the journey from root hair to atmosphere is driven by transpiration's pull - the story of water relations. Water relations covers how plants absorb water through the root hairs, how it rises through the xylem, and how transpiration from the leaves powers the current, plus the osmosis and pressure that manage the movement. The exam asks which force lifts water, which pathway it uses, and what happens when the leaf stomata close. Students lose marks by saying roots pump water, when the pull from the top is the engine. The topic starts Plant Physiology and connects to Photosynthesis, which needs that delivered water, and to Respiration for the sugar traffic in the same pipes. Trace one water molecule from soil to sky in the set below, and the water-relations stems rise with the same current.
subchapters.26|Photosynthesis: A leaf is a solar panel that runs on sunlight, water and the carbon dioxide you breathe out, storing the captured light as sugar - the quiet factory of photosynthesis. Photosynthesis covers the light reaction that splits water and makes energy carries, the dark reaction that fixes carbon into sugar, and the leaf structures that give the process its stage. The exam asks which raw material becomes which product, where each stage of the reaction runs, and what light does to the plant's gas exchange. Students lose marks by darkly naming a dark reaction that needs no light and by losing the products of each stage. The topic depends on Water relations for its supply line and feeds Respiration, which burns the same sugar for energy. Follow the light in and the sugar out in the set below, and the photosynthesis stems turn on the same two-stage current.
subchapters.26|Respiration: Every seed, shoot and root cell burns fuel around the clock, and the sugar built by photosynthesis is the fuel - the quiet burning that powers plant life is respiration. Respiration covers how plants break down glucose to release energy, beginning the process in the cytoplasm and finishing it in the mitochondria, and the aerobic versus anaerobic routes that plants take when oxygen runs short. The exam asks which molecule is oxidized, which organelle finishes the job, and what products each respiration path yields. Students lose marks by treating plant respiration as absent by day, when plants respire at all hours alongside photosynthesis. The topic is the energy mirror of Photosynthesis and connects to Plant growth, which runs on the released energy. Trace the sugar's atoms to carbon dioxide and energy in the set below, and the respiration stems exhale the same balanced equation.
subchapters.26|Plant growth and seed germination: A dormant seed can wait out a winter and burst open in a day when warmth and water arrive, which makes germination the most dramatic moment in a plant's quiet life - and this topic times it. Plant growth and seed germination covers how a seed wakes into a seedling, what conditions trigger and sustain growth, and how plants grow longer at their tips and wider by division. The exam asks which condition a germinating seed needs, which part emerges first and why, and which hormone or factor drives a phase of growth. Students lose marks by blaming soil for a seed that needs only warmth and water, or by confusing growth in length with growth in girth. The topic closes Plant Physiology by applying Water relations and Respiration to the seedling's first days. Follow the seed through wake-up, first root and first leaf in the set below, and the germination stems sprout in the same order.
subchapters.27|Reproduction and sporogenesis in angi: A bee brushing against an anther and a breeze stirring a rice field are both carrying out the same mission - moving pollen, the first step in the flowering plant's hidden reproduction story. Reproduction and sporogenesis in angiosperms follows the whole reproductive cycle in flowers: pollen production, the transfer of pollen to the stigma, the double fertilization inside the ovule, and the spore-producing steps that weave through it. The exam asks which part of the flower performs which role, which structure receives the pollen, and what double fertilization actually produces. Students lose marks by losing the ovule-to-ovary-to-seed chain. The topic hands the next entry's embryo work its raw material, and it connects to Angiosperms and Cell division from earlier chapters. Trace the pollen's journey and the fertilized ovule in the set below, and the reproduction stems bloom along one continuous story.
subchapters.27|Embryo and endosperm: The seed you plant holds a complete miniature plant and a food store wrapped around it, both created by the same double fertilization, and this topic separates the two gifts. Embryo and endosperm covers the development of the embryo from the fertilized egg and the endosperm that nourishes it, naming the parts of the young plant and the tissue that feeds germination. The exam asks which part of the embryo becomes the first root or shoot, how the endosperm is formed, and which seeds store food in the embryo rather than the endosperm. Students lose marks by locating the food store in the wrong tissue. The topic completes Developmental Botany by following Reproduction and sporogenesis to its finished seed, and it connects back to Seed germination's awakening. Separate the baby plant from its lunch once in the set below, and the embryo-endosperm stems split as cleanly as the seed itself.
subchapters.28|Plant tissue culture: Take a single cell from a carrot and grow it into a whole new carrot in a dish - no soil, no seeds, just nutrients and patience - and you have demonstrated plant tissue culture. Plant tissue culture covers the technique of growing plants from cells or tissues on a sterile nutrient medium, producing clones that share the parent's exact traits, and it includes the micropropagation that multiplies rare plants rapidly. The exam asks what a cultured tissue needs, why the offspring of culture are identical, and which problem the technique solves in agriculture. Students lose marks by crediting the technique with creating new traits, when it copies them exactly. The topic opens Applied Botany's modern toolkit and hands Genetic engineering the cells it needs to transform, plus Biofertilizers a place in the same lab. Track one cell to a plantlet in the set below, and the tissue-culture stems grow from the same sterile petri dish.
subchapters.28|Genetic engineering: Move a single gene from a glowing jellyfish into a plant and the plant glows - the ability to cut, copy and paste genes across species is genetic engineering, and this topic explains the scissors, glue and delivery vans. Genetic engineering covers the enzymes that cut DNA at chosen points, the vectors that carry a foreign gene into a host cell, and the transgenic organisms that result, from pest-resistant crops to insulin-making bacteria. The exam asks which enzyme cuts and which joins DNA, what carries the gene into a cell, and which crop or product is genetically modified. Students lose marks by mixing the tool names or by thinking the gene changes the whole cell plan. The topic builds on the DNA and cell work of the Genetics chapter and connects to Plant tissue culture, which grows the transformed cells into plants. Trace one gene from cutting to expression in the set below, and the engineering stems splice together like the DNA itself.
subchapters.28|Biofertilizers and food security: The nitrogen a rice field needs can be pulled from the air by bacteria living on the crop's own roots, which makes biofertilizers a farm input that comes free from nature - and a quiet answer to food security. Biofertilizers and food security covers the living fertilizers - nitrogen-fixing bacteria like Rhizobium, blue-green algae and mycorrhizal fungi - that enrich soil without factory chemicals, and how breeding and biotechnology keep food production ahead of the population curve. The exam asks which organism fixes nitrogen in a crop, which role a named microbe plays in soil, and what food security actually requires. Students lose marks by listing biofertilizers without the mechanism each uses. The topic rounds off Applied Botany and the plant strand itself, connecting Genetic engineering's crops to the field, and it links back to the Economic importance of plant groups. Pair each microbe with its soil service in the set below, and the food-security stems harvest from the same living rows.
subchapters.29|Time and Work: Most CEE aspirants can solve a time-and-work sum alone, then watch the same sum break them when a pipe and a leak enter together - the sign their instinct swapped to guesswork. Time and Work is built on one clean idea: a worker's rate is the fraction of the job done per day, so two workers together add their fractions, and the whole job finishes when the fractions sum to one. The exam's favourite trick hides an agent that works backwards, like a pipe draining the tank that others fill. Students lose marks by abandoning the fraction method and guessing from the raw hours. The topic differs from Time, Speed and Distance, which divides a fixed distance into a fixed time: here the job is a full unit, not a length. Start every stem by naming the fraction per day - one over the time - in the set below, and the work pairs add themselves into one whole job.
subchapters.29|Percentage: A shopkeeper's 20% discount and a bank's 20% interest are not the same 20%, because one shrinks an amount and the other grows it, and that single confusion loses CEE marks by the dozen. Percentage is the exam's most dependable conversion tool: a fraction of a hundred that moves between a number and its per-hundred form, with the change always measured from the starting amount. The exam loves the sequence question - increase, then another increase, then the actual net rise - and the exchange-rate trap where the answer differs by whether the base moves. Students lose marks by adding percentages directly across different bases, which only works when the base stays fixed. The topic feeds Profit and Loss and Simple Interest and Compound Interest, both of which are percentage arithmetic wearing a business suit. Fix the base before every percentage step in the set below, and the per-cents resolve into plain multiplication.
subchapters.29|Profit and Loss: A trader can sell a dozen pens at cost price and still count a profit, because the profit lives in the marker's 10% discount on a 20% marked price - the layered arithmetic that makes profit and loss a trap-and-treat topic. Profit and Loss measures money change around the cost price, with profit and loss as percentages of that single base, and the marked price adding its own discount layer on top. The exam asks the net effect when a seller raises then discounts, which price is the base, and how the profit percent behaves as the cost price changes. Students lose marks by applying the percentage to the selling price instead of the cost, flipping the whole result. The topic is Percentage applied to trade, and it feeds Simple Interest and Compound Interest through the same base-change discipline. Write cost, marked and selling in three rows in the set below, and the profit stems compute themselves top to bottom.
subchapters.29|Ratio and Proportion: When CEE aspirants see three unknowns swinging in a ratio, they often invent numbers out of thin air; the safer move is to give the ratio a concrete unit, and that habit wins the marks. Ratio and Proportion compares two quantities as a single quotient, and proportion extends the comparison to equal ratios, so a ratio like 2 : 3 and its partner 4 : 6 sit on equal terms. The exam's standard move hands a ratio with a total or a difference, and the answer falls out by dividing that total into the ratio's parts. Students lose marks by treating the ratio as the true amount instead of a scaled-down picture of it. The topic is the arithmetic spine of Partnership and Averages, which redistribute a share in the same proportional light. Scale the ratio up to the given total once in the set below, and the proportion stems shrink to a single division.
subchapters.29|Problem on Ages: Can two brothers whose ages add to forty ever be one exactly twice the other, and if so, when? - the curiosity hook that pulls students into age problems before a single formula appears. Problem on Ages turns stated relationships between ages - older by, double of, three-fourths of - into one linear equation, then solves for the unknowns. The exam plants the relations in everyday phrasing and asks for an age now or after a named number of years, so the equation has to hold at the stated time, not at the present. Students lose marks by writing the equation for today and using it for tomorrow. The topic parts company with Averages, which folds many quantities into one representative number, since ages stay individual values throughout. Name the time in the stem first - now, five years ago, after ten years - in the set below, and the age equations set themselves to the right clock.
subchapters.29|Averages: A cricketer who knows his batting average can say how many runs the next innings needs to lift it, because the average already collapsed his whole season into one number - and that single number does real work in this topic. Averages takes a set of values and pools them into one representative figure, and the exam values the reverse move: from the average of a group and its size, recover the total that the average hides. Students lose marks by averaging with an uneven base, such as weighing a 10-day total over 12 days. The topic connects to Percentage, which rescales the same totals, and it feeds the mixed-group sums that appear in the set below. Multiply every average by its group size first in the set below, and the totals surface from each average in one clean multiplication.
subchapters.29|Time, Speed and Distance: A train that passes a pole and a train that passes a whole platform take different times even at identical speed, because the distance to cover differs - and remembering that difference is half the topic. Time, Speed and Distance rests on the single formula that distance equals speed times time, with the subtlety that distance is measured between the relevant points, not the whole journey. The exam's stems convert km/h to m/s, add the train's length to the platform's, and ask for a meeting point of two movers. Students lose marks by leaving units mismatched or by forgetting the object's own length. The topic differs from Time and Work's fraction-per-day method, using fixed distances instead of a single job unit. Convert units and add the two lengths before dividing in the set below, and the speed stems race to the right answer.
subchapters.29|Permutation and Combination: Examiners love this topic because it reads like pure counting, yet asks a question most aspirants cannot phrase: am I arranging, or picking? - and that phrasing is the whole trick. Permutation and Combination counts ways to arrange a set when order matters, and ways to select when it does not, with factorials doing the heavy lifting in both. The exam asks which operation a stem wants, how many ways a group of letters can be arranged with repeats, and whether a committee order counts. Students lose marks by running the factorial for a selection and the combination for an arrangement, inverting the result. The topic draws a clean line against Averages and the other arithmetic chapters, since it counts possibilities rather than measures quantities. Ask whether the stem orders or only selects, in the set below, and the count springs from that single yes-or-no.
subchapters.29|Partnership: Two friends opening a shop together rarely contribute equal money, yet both expect a fair share of profit - the rule that divides the return by their investments is the quiet math of partnership. Partnership divides profit between partners in proportion to their capital and the time it stayed in business, so two rupees invested for three months earn as much as one rupee for six. The exam asks which partner takes which fraction of the profit, folding time in when the investments are not simultaneous. Students lose marks by comparing the capitals alone and forgetting the months. The topic is Ratio and Proportion in business clothing, and it connects to Profit and Loss through the money the partners split. Write each partner's capital-times-time product in the set below, and the profit divides like the ratio of those products.
subchapters.29|Simple Interest and Compound Interest: Borrow a thousand at 10% and you might owe eleven hundred in a year; but leave it two years and compound interest keeps earning on last year's interest, so the two styles drift apart - and students who treat them as one lose the drift. Simple Interest and Compound Interest compute money growth: simple interest pays on the original principal alone, while compound interest pays on the principal plus all interest already earned. The exam asks the difference after two years, the year the gap widens, and how a rate or time halves a principal. Students lose marks by applying the compound formula where the stem clearly says simple, and vice versa. The topic is Percentage and Profit and Loss's arithmetic redirected at lending, with the compounding base changing each year. Track the base - fixed or renewed - in the set below, and the two interests part company at the first year's end.
subchapters.30|Distance and Direction: If you walk three blocks north, turn and walk four east, are you closer to five blocks or seven from where you began? - the right triangle hiding inside every direction puzzle is the curiosity at this topic's core. Distance and Direction maps movement as steps on a compass, and the net displacement falls out of the right triangle those steps trace. The exam walks a person through several turned legs and asks the final distance or the direction faced at the end. Students lose marks by adding lengths that point in different directions instead of resolving them. The topic departs from Coding and Decoding's alphabet rules, using geometry rather than letters. Sketch the path leg by leg, then close the triangle in the set below, and the compass stems land on the spot with Pythagoras.
subchapters.30|Coding and Decoding: The reasoning you refined in Verbal Classification turns playful here: code becomes a small cipher, and the exam rewards the eye that sees the rule behind the letters. Coding and Decoding asks how a word maps to a code through a repeatable rule - shifted letters, reversed order, plus-one positions - and gives you enough examples to infer the rule. The exam presents a coded word, a second word, and asks to encode the third with the same rule. Students lose marks by finding any pattern that fits, when a single coherent rule must hold across both examples. The topic connects to Distance and Direction through shared nerves, both relying on noticing a structure, yet differs by demanding a transformation rather than a figure. Hunt the one consistent rule across both examples in the set below, and the third code falls out as a by-product.
subchapters.30|Ranking Order: Did you know that in a row of students, the person 4th from the front and 7th from the back can still be the middle of the line exactly - and one formula tells you the total? The observation that powers the ranking topic is that fact. Ranking Order resolves positions in a row or list by adding a rank from each end and subtracting the overlap, finding totals and middles from place numbers. The exam gives two ends of one person or two people and asks for the total count or a middle position. Students lose marks by double-counting the shared position or forgetting to subtract it. The topic parts company with Number Series, which runs by arithmetic steps, since ranking runs by counting positions. Add the two ranks and subtract the counted person once in the set below, and the row totals resolve by a single adjustment.
subchapters.30|Verbal Classification: Examiners like this topic because it rewards noticing what ties a list together - and punishes the first similarity that springs to mind, which is usually the trap. Verbal Classification presents four or five words and asks which one does not belong, or which pair shares the missing bond. The exam plants one odd word among four related ones, and the skill is naming the common rule the odd one breaks. Students lose marks by finding a relation that fits the odd word instead of a rule that binds the others. The topic shares its family sense with Verbal Analogy, yet asks for the rule rather than the completion. Name the trait common to all but one word in the set below, and the classification stems reject the intruder by that single shared bond.
subchapters.30|Verbal Analogy: A pen is to writing as a spade is to digging - the everyday pairings we all make without noticing are the raw material of the verbal analogy topic. Verbal Analogy completes the second half of the same relationship the first half begins, asking whether the link is purpose, cause, part-to-whole or another named bond. The exam gives two related words, a third word, and asks which of the options completes the matching pair. Students lose marks by settling for a loose connection when the exam demands the same bond on both sides. The topic grows from Verbal Classification's rule sense while moving from spotting to completing, and it feeds the analogies of Logical Sequencing. Specify the relationship out loud in the set below - what the first pair does - and the matching option must obey that same contract.
subchapters.30|Synonym and Antonym: The classic CEE slip is not forgetting the meaning of a word, but choosing the option that means nearly the same and losing the essential shade - and this topic trains the eye for exactness. Synonym and Antonym tests vocabulary precision: the synonym shares the meaning closely and exactly, while the antonym holds the opposite, and both require rejecting the near-miss distractors. The exam lists one word and four options, at least one a plausible but imprecise cousin. Students lose marks by matching a general sense rather than the precise sense the stem fixes. The topic differs from Verbal Classification's group rules by staying within word meanings, and it feeds the comprehension that Verbal Puzzle exercises. Define the stem word in one plain sentence in the set below, then pick the option that fits that sentence exactly, and the near-miss traps lose their teeth.
subchapters.30|Verbal Puzzle: Can your kitchen clock still tell the correct time if it runs slow - and if it runs slow, which of two clocks is right? These small riddles run on the careful reading this topic trains. Verbal Puzzle presents a scenario with people, objects and conditions, and the solution lives in the precise words, not in arithmetic. The exam asks a conclusion that follows strictly from the given facts, where the tempting option contradicts one stated detail. Students lose marks by importing assumptions the stem never supplied. The topic borrows the logic of Statement and Reasons but drops its formal declarations for a story, and it feeds the puzzles of Logical Sequencing. Underline every stated condition in the set below, and the correct conclusion must obey each underlined line without exception.
subchapters.30|Blood Relations: The reasoning reflexes you built in Ranking Order and Distance and Direction sharpen here: a family tree is a graph, and a blood-relation question is a path through it. Blood Relations traces how one person is related to another through stated links - father of, sister of, wife of - and asks for the relationship that joins two named figures. The exam hands a chain of relations and expects the single word that closes the gap. Students lose marks by reading a relation backwards or by skipping a generation in the chain. The topic shares the step-by-step stamina of Coding and Decoding while operating on family terms, and it feeds the full puzzles of the reasoning chapters. Convert each relation into a labelled arrow in the set below, and the two people connect along the drawn path.
subchapters.30|Statement and Reasons: Did you know that in a well-reasoned argument a true conclusion can still rest on a shaky reason - and the exam loves separating the two? That distinction is the heart of statement and reasons. Statement and Reasons hands a statement, offers reasons that claim to justify it, and asks whether each one truly supports, contradicts or merely accompanies the claim. The exam asks whether the reason explains the statement, repeats it without support, or stands irrelevant to it. Students lose marks by calling any true remark a valid reason, when the reason must actually account for the statement. The topic connects to Verbal Puzzle's careful reading and feeds the analytical reasoning of the later chapter. Check the reason's link to the statement's claim first in the set below - support, repeat or wander - and the verdict writes itself.
subchapters.30|Arithmetical Operation: Examiners like re-coding a normal sum so that plus means minus and minus means times, because it tests whether your arithmetic survives a broken order - the exact stress the arithmetical operation topic applies. Arithmetical Operation replaces the standard symbols with invented meanings and asks you to evaluate an expression under the new rules, and some stems add operator precedence to the confusion. The exam gives a recoded sum and options that range from the normal answer to the correct one. Students lose marks by reverting a re-coded symbol to its usual meaning mid-calculation. The topic leans into the symbol sense of Coding and Decoding while staying in the numeric world, and it feeds the rearrangements of Logical Sequencing. Translate every symbol to its new meaning before evaluating in the set below, and the recoded sums follow purely mechanical arithmetic.
subchapters.31|Number Series: A till in a shop stores the day's takings in a pattern of notes and coins, and a sharp-eyed cashier reads the running total before the count ends - the number series trains the same pattern eye on digits. Number Series presents a sequence and asks the next term, where the rule may add, subtract, multiply or show a square or prime progression. The exam varies the step: constant difference, growing difference, alternating operations, or a skipping pattern. Students lose marks by forcing a single arithmetic step when the sequence alternates operations every other term. The topic is the counting-age partner of Alphabet Series, feeding the same pattern logic with numbers, and it connects to Continuous Patterns as a longer-view version. Test the difference between consecutive terms first in the set below, and the series rule announces itself in one table.
subchapters.31|Alphabet Series: The all-too-common CEE misstep is hunting the alphabet series answer in the letters themselves, when the pattern lives in the letter positions and their jumps - and this topic points the eye to the numbers under the letters. Alphabet Series converts letters to their positions and reads the jumps between them, so A to C is plus two even when the alphabet hides the step. The exam gives a letter run with one position to fill, and the rule may be constant, alternating or symmetric. Students lose marks by straining for a mnemonic instead of writing the positions. The topic mirrors Number Series with the alphabet as its digits, and it feeds the positional work of Continuous Patterns and Positional Series. Write each letter's number beneath it in the set below, and the alphabetical jumps reduce to the number-row logic you already know.
subchapters.31|Continuous Patterns and Positional Se: Can a pattern split cleanly into two interwoven strands that continue on their own - and which strand carries the next term? That split decision is the puzzle of continuous patterns. Continuous Patterns and Positional Series presents an arrangement where two or more separate sequences run side by side, each step counting independently, with the next term depending on which strand is due. The exam gives a long string and asks the term at a far position, or a mixed running pattern, and the solver separates the threads first. Students lose marks by treating the whole string as one sequence when the pattern is woven. The topic extends Number Series and Alphabet Series by doubling the strands, and it feeds the Matrix chapter where the threads run across and down. Tag every term's strand in the set below, and the next term belongs to the strand that is due.
subchapters.31|Matrix and Missing Characters: Every reasoning skill you have banked - the pattern eye from Number Series, the position eye from Alphabet Series - comes together in a grid, and the matrix topic is where the grid appears. Matrix and Missing Characters presents a 3x3 or 2x2 block with one cell empty, and the rule joins the cells across a row or down a column. The exam may want the sum of a row's elements, the product, or a positional relation, and the missing character completes the join. Students lose marks by finding a rule that fits one line while failing the others. The topic synthesizes the series family into two dimensions, and it connects to the figure Matrix of the final chapter with the same grid logic. Check whether the rule binds rows or columns first in the set below, and the missing cell arrives by applying that rule to its own line.
subchapters.31|Analogy: Did you know that the same relationship rule powering verbal analogies runs on words, numbers and figures alike - and the pattern transfers without change? The analogy topic proves that universal reach. Analogy completes a comparable pair across any subject matter: a number pair, a word pair or a figure pair, where the second element obeys the same rule as the first. The exam offers the pair with one blank and options that each echo the given ratio with varying fidelity. Students lose marks by matching the option's look rather than its governing relation. The topic rises from the Verbal Analogy of the earlier chapter and generalizes to pure pattern, feeding the Classification that follows. State the rule between the first two elements in the set below, then hold the options to that rule alone, and the completing pair selects itself.
subchapters.31|Classification: Examiners like this topic because it trains a detective's reflex - pick the odd element by the rule that governs all the others, and the intruder surrenders itself. Classification presents a set of options where one breaks the common rule, and the skill is naming the shared bond the others obey. The exam may present numbers, letters or words, hiding the rule in arithmetic or in the alphabet positions. Students lose marks by finding a private rule that fits the odd element, rather than the set rule the rest share. The topic pairs with the Verbal Classification chapter while moving across number and letter territory, and it connects to the figure Classification Test of the final unit. Find the property common to all but the intruder in the set below, and the classification stems drop the odd element by that single bond.
subchapters.31|Logical Sequence of Words: A dictionary and a recipe both run on order, but one sorts alphabetically and the other by process - and the word-sequence topic asks which order the question demands. Logical Sequence of Words arranges a set of words in a meaningful order, whether by size, stage, hierarchy or the order of an event, and asks the one sequence that fits the stated principle. The exam lists scrambled words and options of orderings, and the correct one obeys the named logic. Students lose marks by imposing alphabetical order where the stem clearly wants process order. The topic connects to Ranking Order's positional reasoning while adding a meaning requirement, and it feeds the sequencing of the whole chapter. Ask what principle the stem names - size, process, time - in the set below, and the order arranges itself under that rule.
subchapters.31|Logical Venn-Diagram: The classic CEE stumble in Venn questions is testing set membership with a guess instead of a diagram, and the diagram instantly reveals the three-way house the sets build. Logical Venn-Diagram uses overlapping circles to show how categories include, exclude and share members, reading the overlapping zones as the elements that belong to two or three sets at once. The exam shows a diagram of three interlocking circles and asks which region a named item occupies. Students lose marks by reading the outer circle alone and missing the intersections. The topic applies the classification logic of the earlier chapters in spatial form, and it feeds the analytical reasoning puzzles of the final unit. Mark each item into the smallest region that contains it in the set below, and the Venn stems resolve by one placement each.
subchapters.31|Common Properties: What do a spoon, a fork and a knife share - and which of their cousins fails the test? The common-properties topic turns that everyday grouping into a reasoning skill. Common Properties asks which option shares the property that binds a given set, finding the trait all the listed elements hold. The exam presents a group and options, one of which belongs through the common rule while the others miss it. Students lose marks by naming a property so broad that every option qualifies. The topic is Classification working in the co-operative direction - finding the bond rather than the intruder - and it connects to the figure Grouping of the final unit. State the shared property precisely, then test every option against it exactly in the set below, and the common item steps forward by the property alone.
subchapters.32|Series: The reasoning reflexes you sharpened in the Number and Alphabet series carry over here, with the sequence now drawn instead of written - a figure shifts, turns or multiplies into the next frame. Series in figures presents a chain of diagrams and asks for the frame that continues the transformation. The exam's figure rules include rotation, addition, shading and movement, and the solver names the one rule the frames obey. Students lose marks by searching the whole picture when the change lives in a single element. The topic imports the pattern logic of the earlier series chapters into the spatial world, and it feeds the Matrix and Classification Test of this unit. Isolate the one element that changes between frames in the set below, and the next figure follows that single move.
subchapters.32|Classification Test: Did you know that the odd-one-out test works on figures exactly as it does on words - and four similar pictures plus one intruder make a complete classification stem? The figure classification test confirms that. Classification Test presents four figures sharing a transformation or property and asks which breaks the rule, where the bonded rule may be of symmetry, rotation or shading. The exam plants the intruder by a small deviation that most eyes miss. Students lose marks by choosing the figure that merely looks different instead of the one that breaks the shared rule. The topic is the Verbal Classification of the earlier chapter redrawn as shapes, feeding the Figure Formation that follows. Name the common property of three figures in the set below, and the odd figure is the one that violates it.
subchapters.32|Analogy: The very rule that completed word and number analogies completes the visual line: a figure transforms into its partner, and the next pair must obey the same move. The figure analogy topic proves the rule travels across a picture. Analogy in figures pairs one figure with its transformed version - rotated, reversed, rescaled - and asks which option shows the same transformation applied to a new figure. The exam can flip, mirror or combine elements, and the solver isolates the deformation that the first pair displays. Students lose marks by matching the option's shape rather than its transformation. The topic connects the verbal analogy logic to the spatial world and feeds the Matrix figures of this unit. Name the operation the first pair performs in the set below, apply it to the third figure, and the answer is the transformed twin of the given shape.
subchapters.32|Matrix: The grid logic that solved figure matrices in the earlier reasoning chapters continues here, but now every cell is a drawing, and the empty cell waits for the picture that completes both its row and column. The figure Matrix topic presents a 3x3 grid of images with one empty, where the rule may run across a row or down a column, and the correct answer must obey whichever direction the pattern actually follows. Students lose marks by solving only half the rule and letting the other half fail, or by finding a rule that happens to fit the row while contradicting the column. The topic multiplies the Classification and Analogy logic into two dimensions, since every cell must satisfy both axes at once, and it feeds the Figure Formation that assembles pieces into wholes. Check rows and columns separately in the set below, and the missing figure must respect both directions of the pattern before it earns its place.
subchapters.32|Figure Formation: A jigsaw's pieces assemble into one picture, and the figure-formation topic asks the same assembly in the exam - which two or more small figures combine to make a given shape. Figure Formation shows a target outline and a set of components, asking which combination of the parts composes it exactly. The exam may require superimposing, adjoining or fitting figures, with only one option matching the target's complete geometry. Students lose marks by matching the areas and ignoring the orientation of a component. The topic builds on the pieces-and-wholes logic of the verbal puzzles, translating it into construction, and it connects to Construction of Figure that follows. Test each option by fitting its pieces against the target's outline in the set below, and the one exact assembly clicks into place.
subchapters.32|Construction of Figure: Can two simple shapes, slid and rotated, rebuild a complex silhouette exactly - and which of the given combinations closes the picture? Construction of Figure makes the visual answer the test. This topic shows a target figure and options of component groups, asking which set, aligned and combined, reproduces the target's full outline without gaps, overlaps or dangling edges. Students lose marks by choosing the option whose pieces have the same count rather than the same shape fit, or by ignoring how a piece must be turned before it slots in. The topic pairs with Figure Formation, sharing the assemble-to-target logic while allowing searching, and it feeds the Analytical Reasoning Test's figure logic with the same careful assembly. Overlay each option's pieces mentally on the target in the set below, and only the option that covers every corner of the silhouette survives the fit.
subchapters.32|Analytic Reasoning Test: The calm, step-ladder reasoning you practised in Statement and Reasons and Logical Sequence of Words returns in a figure-free, purely verbal frame: a set of conditions and a question that one deductive chain settles. Analytic Reasoning Test hands a small scenario with several stated conditions and asks which conclusion must follow. The exam expects a single necessary consequence, and the correct option is the one fully guaranteed by the given facts. Students lose marks by picking a plausible option that the conditions permit but do not force. The topic distils the earlier verbal logic chapters into pure deduction, and it precedes the grouping and folding figure types that end the unit. Write every stated condition as a firm line in the set below, and the answer must be true under all of them simultaneously.
subchapters.32|Grouping Figure: The four-figure classification eye you trained in Classification Test reappears here, but the figures now divide into sets: the grouping figure topic sorts images into two families by one shared rule. Grouping Figure presents several figures and asks which can be grouped, or which partitions them into the two sets their properties imply. The exam's decisive trait may be symmetry, open versus closed shapes, or shading, and the solver names the rule that sorts all of them. Students lose marks by grouping by appearance while letting the underlying rule shift between pairs. The topic connects the Classification logic to arrangement, feeding the Embedded Figure work that follows. Declare the sorting rule before grouping in the set below, and every figure lands in its family under the same rule.
subchapters.32|Paper Folding: Examiners like paper-folding because it needs no calculation and rewards spatial patience: one fold, a punched hole, and the unfolded sheet must show the mirrored holes. Paper Folding presents a sheet, a fold line and a punched position, and asks which unfolded result retains the correct mirrored pattern. The exam starts from simple single folds and climbs to stacked sheets, where each hole mirrors across every crease. Students lose marks by picturing the hole where punched and forgetting its reflections. The topic shares the mirror instinct of Water Image and Mirror Image and feeds the Cube and Dice work through the same mental rotation. Fold the sheet mentally one crease at a time in the set below, and the hole pattern emerges by reflecting each punch across each fold.
subchapters.32|Cube and Dice: A dice thrown on a table can show one face at a time, yet experienced players can name the hidden faces by the opposite-face rule - the same rule that powers the cube-and-dice topic. Cube and Dice answers questions about visible and hidden faces: opposite faces never appear together, and adjacent ones always do. The exam shows a cube in two or more views and asks which face sits opposite a given one, or how a net folds into a cube. Students lose marks by memorizing twist sequences instead of applying the opposite-face rule. The topic builds on Paper Folding's spatial turns and connects to the Embedded Figure eye of this unit. Fix the opposite-face pairs from the views in the set below, and each cube question resolves by elimination.
subchapters.32|Embedded Figure: A hidden tiger in a forest photograph reveals itself once the eye knows its outline, and the embedded-figure topic trains exactly that contour-hunting eye on the exam. Embedded Figure shows a target figure and a larger complex figure in which the target hides, asking where the small shape is embedded. The exam may rotate or scale the target inside its host, so the outline match matters more than position. Students lose marks by matching an outline that only partly overlaps the target. The topic borrows the search discipline of Figure Formation while moving from assembly to detection, and it connects to the Dot Situation logic. Trace the target's full outline across the host in the set below, and the embedded figure announces itself where the edges coincide.
subchapters.32|Dot Situation: Can a single isolated dot lie inside two named regions of a figure at once - and read the figure's overlaps to say where it sits? That placement reading is the dot-situation puzzle. Dot Situation presents a figure with overlapping regions and a small dot located somewhere, asking which set of regions the dot belongs to by its position inside their intersections. Students lose marks by counting the regions without reading which loops enclose the dot. The topic pairs with the Embedded Figure's region logic while focusing on containment, and it folds the whole spatial chapter's placement skills into one question type. Identify every closed region enclosing the dot in the set below, and the answer names exactly that combination of loops.
subchapters.32|Water Image and Mirror Image: The reflection instinct you practised in Paper Folding sharpens further here: a mirror flips a word's letters sideways, while water reverses them top to bottom, and each image obeys a strict flip axis. Water Image and Mirror Image presents a word or figure and asks which option is its correct mirror reflection, and some stems ask for the water-image separately. The exam's trap reverses only some of the letters or flips along the wrong axis. Students lose marks by flipping the whole word while turning individual letters the wrong way. The topic connects to Cube and Dice through the shared spatial-turn logic, and it closes the spatial reasoning of this unit. Fix the axis - vertical for mirror, horizontal for water - in the set below, then reverse each letter along that axis, and the correct image reflects itself.

sets.1|1: A cyclist rounding a bend keeps her balance by leaning inward, a truck's wheels skid before its tyres give, and a satellite never falls because it keeps missing the ground - every one of these is Mechanics in the real world, and this first set walks you through its worked solutions. Mechanics is best attacked with a formula-first discipline: read the question, list what is given and what is asked, choose the equation that connects them, then substitute with units intact. In this set you will meet the full range of the unit, from Kinematics and Dynamics to Rotational dynamics and Circular and Periodic motion, so expect one method per question type and no wander. Attempt each numbered solution before reading its worked answer, then compare your chosen formula against the model - the fastest way to erase a bad habit. Watch the recurring trap of units, especially the second squared that hides in acceleration answers. Work through set by set in order below, and the recurring formulas will start announcing themselves before you finish reading a stem.
sets.1|2: A stone dropped down a well, a bridge that sags under a lorry, and a ball that floats in water all answer to the same book of rules, and this is the set where those rules are solved in public. In Mechanics the reliable habit is to draw the situation - axes, forces, and velocities - before touching any formula, because a small diagram makes the other half of the stem obvious. The worked solutions here cover Dynamics and Gravity as well as Elasticity and Fluid statics and dynamics, and you will see how the same vector discipline that resolves a force also resolves a velocity or a momentum. Before you look at a worked solution, sketch the diagram the model would draw, then check whether your arrows match. The mistake this unit punishes most is dropping a sign: a vector pointing the other way changes answers by a factor that no calculator can repair. Read the solutions in the set below with a pencil in hand, and the reasoning behind each equation will belong to you after the first handful of stems.
sets.1|3: A spinning cricket ball curves through the air, a rotating wheel tightens a rope, and a gyroscope refuses to fall until it runs down - the rotational half of the world is all Mechanics, and this set carries its solutions. The surest approach to rotational questions is to translate from the linear vocabulary you already know: force becomes torque, mass becomes moment of inertia, and the same kinematic formulas wear new names. In this set you will solve for Rotational dynamics, Circular and Periodic motion, and the vector method of Physical quantities, vectors and scalars that underpins every diagram in the chapter. Take each stem on its own terms first, converting rotation to its linear twin before picking an equation. Many aspirants halve their marks by writing Newton's second law for the centre of mass and never noticing the rotation involved. Move through the worked problems in the set below, and the rotational mirror of the mechanics formulas will start answering at sight.
sets.1|4: A tightrope walker's pole, the sway of a tall building in the wind, and the crisper curve of a racing track all rest on the handful of equations solved in this set's worked pages. Mechanics rewards a strict order of operations: identify the body, list every force on it, then resolve them along chosen axes before any arithmetic begins. The stems here concentrate on Rotational dynamics, Circular and Periodic motion, and the coupled problems of Elasticity and Fluid statics and dynamics, so the solutions show how each formula is picked, not just applied. Use the set as a check rather than a first read - attempt each item, then open its worked answer and look for the single assumption you made that the model did not. The most common slip in this material is treating frequency and angular velocity as the same number when their factor of two pi separates them. Work through the set below in one calm sitting, and the mechanics equations will settle into a short list you can trust.
sets.1|5: A goalkeeper judging the dip of a long shot, an engineer rating a bridge for its load, and a doctor measuring blood pressure with a column of mercury are all doing formal Mechanics without naming it, and this set explains every step. The approach that serves best here is elimination by quantity: decide whether the stem asks about motion, force, energy, or the static balance of a body, and the candidate formulas narrow themselves. This set's worked solutions draw on the broad sweep of the unit - Dynamics, Elasticity, Gravity, and Fluid statics and dynamics - so you will see the shared vector grammar that runs through each. Answer each problem mentally before exposing the solution, and write your own given-asked-answer list for the harder items. The recurring trap is assuming a body is in equilibrium when the stem has not said so, which plants a wrong zero where an acceleration belongs. Enter the set below with that checklist ready, and the mechanics stems will stop springing surprises.
sets.2|1: Tea cools because heat leaves it, a steam engine runs because heat flows from flame to boiler, and a fridge moves heat uphill with work - the direction traffic of heat is the whole story, and this first set walks its solutions. Thermodynamics is best handled sequentially: name the process, note what is held constant, then apply the corresponding law rather than quoting them all at once. The stems here range across the Second law of thermodynamics, the Ideal gas equation, and Thermal expansion, so the solutions model how each law is recognized from its signature phrase. Before reading a worked answer, name which law the stem is asking about, and only then compare with the model. The classic loss here is removing or adding heat while forgetting the sign convention, which flips every later number. Take the set below question by question, and the three laws will sort themselves by the process each stem describes.
sets.2|2: A room fills with the everyday steam of a kettle, a bicycle pump grows warm as air is compressed, and a glass cracks when boiling water meets cold - each is a different chapter of the same heat story, and this set untangles them. The method that wins here is constant-spotting: identify which quantity stays fixed, and the process - isothermal, isobaric or adiabatic - states its own governing equation. You will solve for the First law of thermodynamics and its energy bookkeeping, the Ideal gas behaviour, and Thermal energy, heat, temperature and thermometers, seeing how one energy balance serves all three. Try each item first and write the first law in terms of the given quantities before peeking at the worked solution. Aspirants routinely bleed marks by treating heat and temperature as the same variable, when heat is transferred energy and temperature is the reading. Step into the set below, and the processes will start identifying themselves before you reach the answer line.
sets.2|3: The same cup of coffee that warms your palm through a steel spoon does so quickly, while a wooden spoon stays cool - the conducitivity contrast behind everyday decisions is the theme of this solutions set. This unit rewards a vocabulary-first approach: translate the stem's everyday words into thermodynamic quantities - heat, work, internal energy - and the law that applies chooses itself. The worked solutions here cover the First law of thermodynamics, the Ideal gas equation, and Quantity of heat, so the patterns of a standard calorimetry or gas question become visible within a few examples. Do each stem before opening its worked answer, then check whether you and the model applied the same law, not merely the same arithmetic. The trap this set exposes is mixing up which quantities are path-dependent and which are state functions, a distinction that decides whole marks. Read the questions in the set below in order, and the thermodynamic vocabulary will start translating on sight.
sets.2|4: A chilled bottle on a warm day gathers dew, inflated tyres harden after a long drive, and a hot lid cannot be twisted loose - three everyday dramas, one thermodynamic script, all solved in this set. The dependable route here is bookkeeping first: track the flows of heat, the work done, and the internal energy change, and the First law of thermodynamics closes the accounts. This set's solutions work through the Second law of thermodynamics, the Ideal gas equation, and Thermal expansion, showing how the direction rules and the gas law combine in a single exam question. Attempt each stem, write your three-line ledger before the solution, and compare only after your own numbers exist. The most costly habit is appealing to entropy without explaining which direction the process may take, which the exam punishes directly. Work the set below with the energy ledger open, and the thermodynamic stems balance themselves.
sets.2|5: A solar panel's flat face, a hypothermia victim's shiver, and a sky full of hot-air balloons all rely on how heat moves and stores itself, and this set lays out the worked path through the ideas. Start from the thermometer: decide what is constant, what flows, and what changes, and the process names itself, which is the core thermostat habit of this unit. The solutions here span the First law of thermodynamics, the Ideal gas equation, and Quantity of heat, so you will see the shared energy-accounting threading through distinct problem types in one sitting. Solve each item independently first, then compare - the set rewards the attempt far more than the reading. The hallmark mistake of this chapter is using a gas formula on a liquid or a solid without checking the state, which quietly corrupts the number. Meet the questions in the set below after that one check, and the heat questions will stay as predictable as the laws themselves.
sets.3|1: A distant thunderclap reaches your ears after its flash, ripples spread over a pond, and two speakers can cancel at a seat where neither alone is heard - the choreography of waves is everywhere, and this set solves it step by step. The productive method in waves is to fix the medium first: the wave speed, its frequency, and wavelength settle there, and almost every formula in the unit hangs on those three. The worked pages here cover Interference, Diffraction and polarization, and Reflection, refraction and dispersion, so you will watch the same superposition idea operate on light and on sound. Try each question with your own sketch before the solution, marking crests and troughs, and then compare the model's diagram with yours. The classic trap is doubling the path difference when the question already did, or forgetting the half-wavelength flip at a fixed end. Move through the set below and the wave relationships will fix themselves in a small set of dependable ratios.
sets.3|2: Crossing a railway line you hear the horn climb and fall as the train passes, and a thin film on water shows rainbow stripes - Doppler shift and interference are camouflage for the same wave math, and this set exhibits it. The winning approach here is to identify the quantity the stem asks about and then resolve the waves into their measurable parts, frequency, wavelength, and speed, before applying any relation. This set's solutions focus on Acoustic phenomena, Interference, and Stationary waves, showing how a standing wave's nodes mark half the story. Read each question, predict the answer's size and sign before computing, then open the worked response and check both the number and the reasoning. Aspirants give up marks when they use a formula for travelling waves on a standing-wave question, where the boundaries change everything. Work through the set below and the acoustic and interference patterns will stop looking like different subjects.
sets.3|3: A cinema screen your voice bounces off, the sparkle of a diamond, and a choir's note that swells in a high hall all demonstrate the reflection, refraction and spreading of waves that this set solves by hand. The method that carries this unit is ray geometry first: trace the path of the wave or light, mark the angles at every surface, and let Snell's law and the wave relations do the rest. In these worked solutions you will meet Wave motion, Diffraction and polarization, and the grinding of diffraction through a slit, with the same language serving sound and light alike. Attempt each stem from your own diagram before the solution, and only then check how the model bent the same ray. The recurring loss here is switching the indices of refraction, which flips the whole bending direction and marks every later step wrong. Step into the set below with the ray already drawn, and the optics stems will refract toward the correct option by themselves.
sets.3|4: The shimmer of a mirage, the deep tone a flute drops into, and the clear ring of a struck bell each trace back to waves meeting boundaries, and this set walks the solutions to those meetings. The habit to build here is symmetry-spotting: waves that reflect at a fixed end invert, and waves that reflect at a free end do not, a single contrast that resolves half the chapter. The worked solutions cover Stationary waves, Acoustic phenomena, and Reflection, refraction and dispersion, threading the same boundary logic through each problem type. Solve each item cold, then compare your boundary choices with the model's before you check any arithmetic. The mark-bleeding error in this group is treating a fixed end and a free end with the same reflection rule, which quietly reverses the harmonic sequence. Descend into the set below one question at a time, and the boundary rules will assert themselves as the unit's true skeleton.
sets.3|5: A radar dish collects returning echoes, a sunglass lens dims glare, and a guitar string holds a note fixed by its own waves - this set exhibits the solutions that tie detection, polarization and standing waves into one mechanics of vibration. The approach that succeeds here is to locate the pattern first: whether the question describes a moving disturbance, an interference pattern, or a fixed standing shape decides the toolbox before any formula is quoted. In these pages you will see Diffraction and polarization, Stationary waves, and Interference worked alongside each other, the better to hear their shared vocabulary. Take each stem without notes, confirm whether you named the same phenomenon as the model, and only then check the numbers. The most common slip is describing a diffraction pattern where the stem describes interference, two ideas the exam loves to contrast in one option list. Engage the set below, and the wave phenomena will separate into clear, non-overlapping boxes in your memory.
